1. To approach means to come physically closer, to come near: when Moses approaches the burning bush or when the people approach the altar to bring an offering (Leviticus 1:2).

2. To bring someone near to another is to lead them to him: Moses must bring Aaron and his sons near to consecrate them to the priesthood (Exodus 28:1), or the priest brings the sacrificial animal to the altar (Leviticus 1:3).

3. To present an offering to God means to solemnly bring it before Him to give it to Him: the faithful will "present" a flawless animal (Leviticus 3:12), a portion of flour, or other goods to the Lord.

4. To offer means to give as a gift, to deliver what belongs to someone else: one "offers" to the Lord sacrifices consumed by fire (Leviticus 23:8) in recognition of His lordship and our dependence.

5. To put forward or propose a word, a supplication, a prayer: to approach God is also to present our requests and our hearts to Him.
H7126H.origine: The Hebrew verb קָרַב comes from a root that expresses the idea of coming closer, of crossing a distance. The fundamental word is related to the image of movement towards a person or a place. In biblical Hebrew, the same root produces names like קָרְבָן (qorban), the offering or sacrifice — what is "brought near" to God. The meaning has enriched: to approach God through an offering is to stand before Him with respect and submission.
H7126H.emploi: This verb appears 155 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in Leviticus and Exodus, where it describes the Temple liturgy. In its literal sense, it means to approach or bring someone near: to bring Aaron near (Exodus 28:1), to bring the sons of Aaron near (Leviticus 8:24). In a cultic sense, very frequent, it designates the act of presenting a sacrifice or an offering to God: to offer an animal (Leviticus 1:3), to offer flour (Leviticus 2:1), to offer a sacrifice for seven days (Leviticus 23:8). The word also applies to the respectful approach to the sanctuary: to approach to serve, to consecrate oneself. In all cases, the key idea is that of drawing near — physically or morally — before the presence of God or an authority.
H7126H.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that access to God is not natural: we must approach with an offering, a right intention, and respect. In the Old Testament, the sacrifice is the institutional means of approaching God; the Christian sees in Jesus the ultimate offering that brings us definitively closer to the Father. To offer to the living God is to give Him what matters most — our possessions, our time, our hearts — in recognition of His authority and grace.

sens: To come physically closer to someone or something
To come to present something, especially an offering or a sacrifice
To appear before someone, to present oneself to him
H7127.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to come physically closer: Nebuchadnezzar approached the entrance of the furnace to see the three young men (Daniel 3:26). It is a movement in space, coming near to someone or something.
2. A very important ritual sense: to offer sacrifices or offerings to God. The Jews offered bulls, rams, and lambs for the dedication of the house of God (Ezra 6:17). The verb implies not only a physical approach to the altar but the solemn act of presenting an offering to God.
3. To appear or present oneself before an authority: the Chaldeans approached the king to accuse him (Daniel 3:8), or men presented themselves before the king regarding a royal decree (Daniel 6:12). It is to come to show oneself to someone of higher rank.
H7127.origine: The Hebrew word qerev fundamentally expresses the idea of coming closer or coming near. It is used mainly in the Aramaic texts of Daniel and Ezra (the Aramaic part of the biblical canon). The notion of offering is naturally related: bringing an offering to the altar means coming closer to it. The forms vary (P'al, Pael, Aphel) depending on whether the action is simple, the act of bringing near, or presenting ritually.
H7127.emploi: This verb appears 9 times in the provided usages, mainly in Ezra and Daniel. In Ezra (6:10, 6:17, 7:17), it almost always means to offer sacrifices or offerings to God in a liturgical context: the exiles restore the temple worship. In Daniel (3:8, 3:26, 6:12, 6:20, 7:13, 7:16), it alternates between physical approach (to come near to someone or a place) and the act of presenting oneself before an authority (the king, the Most High). The legal or heavenly vision context gives the verb a particular solemnity.
H7127.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that approaching God is never trivial: it is coming with respect and with an offering (our prayers, our lives). The Epistle to the Hebrews will explore this theme by showing that Christ is our only high priest who allows us to approach God. This word also roots the idea that appearing before God or before the authority He establishes requires reverence and honesty.

sens: Armed confrontation between warriors or armies
Struggle, conflict, or tension between enemies
Threatening approach or presence of adversaries
H7128.detail:
1. The primary meaning is organized military confrontation: combatants face to face, soldiers ready for battle. In 2 Samuel 17:11, David proposes to march "in person to the battle" with all Israel, and in Psalms 78:9, the sons of Ephraim "turned back on the day of battle" — they fled the confrontation. It is the battle itself, with its weapons and stakes.
2. The word also designates war in a broader sense, the state of prolonged conflict or the activity of fighting. In Job 38:23, God withholds "for the days of war and battle" hail and storms; in Psalms 68:31, God "scatters the peoples who take pleasure in fighting" — it is the propensity for war, the love of conflict.
3. Sometimes the word evokes only the threat or presence of the enemy. In Psalms 55:19, the psalmist says, "He will deliver me from their approach" — here, the battle is not fought, but the hostile approach of the adversary causes fear. It is the danger that comes toward us.
H7128.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of coming closer or being near: combat is when enemies come closer to each other, face to face. This image of drawing near also explains why the word can mean "approach" in the sense of a threatening presence. It is a concrete and vivid word in biblical Hebrew, very common in war narratives and psalms.
H7128.emploi: The word appears 9 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the Psalms and historical narratives. It designates either the armed combat itself (2 Samuel 17:11; Psalms 78:9), or war as a general reality (Job 38:23; Psalms 55:22), or simply the threat and approach of the enemy (Psalms 55:19). The context shows that it can be physical and direct or symbolic and moral: the "war" of the heart in Psalms 55:22 is that of deceptive speech. It is a word of ordinary human experience and images of combat that everyone understands.
H7128.portee: This word reminds the believer that life involves real or spiritual battles, and that deliverance comes from God alone. The psalms that use it express legitimate fear in the face of danger and trust in divine protection. It helps the reader to see that God knows our struggles and that He can free us from them.

sens: Armed conflict between peoples or kings
Direct combat between warriors
Sustained struggle or opposition
H7129.detail:
1. The word designates an organized armed conflict, what nations do when they confront each other militarily. In Daniel 7:21, the little horn "makes war on the saints," which shows a violent and prolonged opposition directed against the people of God.
2. It can also evoke a more direct, face-to-face combat between warriors or fighters engaged on a battlefield.
3. Figuratively, the word applies to any sustained struggle or opposition between opposing forces, such as that waged by the enemies of the people of God.
H7129.origine: This Aramaic word comes from the root קרב (qara·b), which means "to approach" or "to be near." War is when enemies approach each other to confront. It is the same word as in classical Hebrew, qerav (קְרָב), which has the same meaning. The basic idea is that of hostile proximity: two armies drawing near to fight.
H7129.emploi: This Aramaic word appears only once in the New Testament, in Daniel 7:21. Daniel reports his vision of a little horn that "makes war on the saints and prevails over them." Here, the war is not an ordinary conflict between kingdoms, but a religious persecution directed against the people of God. It is a spiritual struggle described in terms of political and military conflict, which underscores the intensity and reality of the battle that the faithful must face.
H7129.portee: This passage reminds believers that opposition to the people of God is real and organized, and that it takes the form of a genuine struggle. But the context shows that, despite this temporal war, God intervenes and establishes His eternal kingdom: what seems to be a victory for the enemy is only temporary and does not last.

sens: The central space of a group, city, assembly
Among, in the heart of, within (with the idea of participation or proximity)
The interior of the body, the innards or vital organs
The seat of emotions, thoughts, conscience (the moral heart)
H7130G.detail:
1. The midst designates the central space occupied by a person or object: Abraham asks if God would spare the city if there were fifty righteous in the "midst" of Sodom (Genesis 18:24), referring to the geographical center of the city.

2. Among or within marks active presence or participation: the Lord is "in the midst" of His people as one who guides and protects them (Numbers 14:14), or a people passes "among" the other nations (Joshua 24:17). This notion includes the idea of being surrounded, involved, in direct relationship.

3. The interior of the body, particularly the innards or viscera: in the Hebrew language, "qerev" refers to the vital organs, and in the context of sacrifices, it is the internal offering portion of the animal (Leviticus 17:4).

4. The heart as the seat of emotion, conscience, or thought: when the psalmist says that his heart is wounded "within" him (Psalms 109:22), he speaks of his inner and moral suffering, not just physical.
H7130G.origine: The Hebrew word "qerev" (קֶרֶב) comes from a root that fundamentally means "the inside" or "what is at the center." The image starts from the body (the innards as the center of life) and extends to anything that is at the center or midst of a group, place, or situation. This progression from the concrete to the figurative is typical of Hebrew thought: the body and its organs serve as a model to speak of spiritual and emotional reality. The same root gives rise to other words related to interiority and centrality.
H7130G.emploi: The word "qerev" appears 196 times in the Old Testament, primarily in the Torah and historical books. Its most frequent usage is spatial: designating the midst or center of a city, camp, assembly (Genesis 18:24, Deuteronomy 21:9). It is also used to express the divine presence among the people: "the Lord is in the midst of you" becomes an affirmation of divine protection and accompaniment (Numbers 14:14). A third register is that of moral and emotional interiority: the "qerev" becomes the seat of feelings, reflection, guilt (Leviticus 20:3, Psalms 109:22). The translation varies according to context: "midst" for physical or social space, "within" or "inside" for interiority, "bosom" to express the intimacy of a relationship.
H7130G.portee: This word teaches that the presence of God in the midst of His people is not abstract: it is real, tangible, close. It also invites us to recognize that our emotions, thoughts, and guilt are not hidden — they inhabit our "interior" that God sees and knows. For the believer, the "qerev" reminds us that God is never distant, but at the very heart of our lives and communities.

sens: Viscera and internal organs of a sacrificed animal
Internal depth of the body or human heart, seat of emotions
Heart considered as the center of thought, reflection, and intention
Midst, center, or interior of a group, assembly
H7130H.detail:
1. In the sacrifices of Israel, the word designates the viscera of the animal: the Bible speaks of washing the innards before burning them on the altar (Leviticus 1:9), or the fat attached to the innards, offered to the Lord (Leviticus 3:14). It is the concrete anatomy of the sacrifice.

2. By natural extension, the word applies to the inside of the human body as the seat of strong feelings: the psalmists speak of an "intimate thought" or a "heart" filled with malice (Psalms 5:10, Psalms 64:7). The innards then symbolize what is deepest, most hidden within a person.

3. The word also designates intention, plan, inner meditation: enemies "meditate crimes, conceive a plan" in their innards (Psalms 64:7), meaning they ruminate, they reflect in secret.

4. Finally, "innards" can simply mean "in the midst of," "among," designating the interior of a group or space: speaking "in the midst" of an assembly.
H7130H.origine: The Hebrew word קֶרֶב (qérev) comes from a root designating interiority, what is within. In biblical Hebrew, it is very close to the concept of "heart" (לֵב, lév), but with an emphasis on the physical aspect — the viscera — before applying to the seat of emotions and thoughts. This evolution from the concrete to the figurative is very common in Hebrew: one would start with the reality of the sacrifice, then extend the image to the invisible human dimensions.
H7130H.emploi: The word appears 24 times in the Hebrew Bible. It is omnipresent in the sacrificial laws of Leviticus (Leviticus 1, 3, 4, 7, 8, 9), where it precisely designates the viscera of the burnt offering animal: liver, kidneys, fat of the innards. In the Psalms, its usage becomes deeper: it describes the secret place of malice (Psalms 5:10), intimate thoughts (Psalms 64:7), the inner agitation of the soul (Psalms 94:19). The transition from physical meaning to psychological meaning is gradual and natural: the image of the body is used to speak of the soul.
H7130H.portee: This word teaches the believer that nothing is hidden from God: not only our visible acts, but our most secret thoughts, nestled deep within our "innards," remain transparent before the Lord. It also reminds us of the importance of the heart and intention in biblical faith: what matters is not the outward appearance, but what resides within a person.

sens: to advance near something or someone
to come into contact, to enter the sacred space of the sanctuary
to walk towards, to head in a direction
to be close, to be nearby
H7131.detail:
1. The fundamental meaning is that of a physical movement: to advance, to reduce the distance that separates one from someone or something. It is the action of one who walks towards a goal or a person. Examples: in 1 Samuel 17:41, Goliath "approaches" David to confront him; in 2 Samuel 18:25, the watchman sees a runner "approaching".

2. In the context of Israelite worship, "approach" takes on a very specific and serious meaning: it is to enter the sacred space of the tabernacle or temple to draw near or touch its objects. Only the priests and Levites had the right to approach the sanctuary; anyone else who "approaches" will be put to death (Numbers 1:51, 3:10, 18:7). It is a religious boundary that separates the profane from the sacred.

3. The verb can also simply mean "to go towards", "to head" in a more general sense, without religious connotation (Deuteronomy 20:3: the Israelites "go" to battle).

4. Rarely, the word expresses the idea of being close, being in proximity to something, in an almost adjectival sense.
H7131.origine: The word comes from a Semitic root that expresses the idea of forward movement, of drawing near. In Hebrew, this root is also used to designate the front, the face, that which is face to face. The Levites who "approach" the tabernacle are those who are charged with it, who serve it in front (Ezekiel 40:46, 45:4). The notion of approach often contains an issue of dangerous or forbidden proximity: to approach the sacred without right was fatal.
H7131.emploi: The word appears 11 times in biblical Hebrew. In the provided usages, the majority of occurrences (5 out of 6 in Numbers) concern access to the tabernacle: it is a fundamental legal and religious term of the Torah. The verb is used in the participle form ("the one who approaches") to designate one who transgresses the prohibition. A few more general usages appear: to approach in battle (1 Samuel 17:41), to approach the king or a notable (2 Samuel 18:25), to approach for service (1 Kings 4:27). The meaning always remains that of a movement towards a place, a person, or a specific action.
H7131.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that access to God was not trivial in Israel: it required mediation, consecration, holiness. In the Old Testament, approaching God was reserved for the priests. This restriction prepares the revelation of the New Testament: through Christ, all believers can now "approach with confidence the throne of grace" (Hebrews 4:16). The word invites reflection on the privilege and responsibility of accessing the divine presence.

sens: the act of drawing near, coming close
the movement towards someone or something
access to God, personal relationship with Him
H7132.detail:
1. The word designates the action of physically drawing near, the movement of one who advances towards a goal. In Psalms 73:28, the psalmist says that for him, "drawing near to God" is good, which means establishing an intimate relationship with the Lord, seeking His presence.
2. More broadly, it is access, the possibility of coming close to someone. In Isaiah 58:2, when people "desire the approach of God", they seek to have access to Him, to meet Him and hear His voice.
3. The word also evokes intimacy and communion: to draw near to God is not a mere religious formality, but a personal act of love and trust, a desire for true relationship.
H7132.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to be near, to draw close". It is formed on the same base as other words expressing proximity and nearness. The starting image is that of physical movement towards someone or something. In the Old Testament, this vocabulary of approach characterizes the relationship between man and God: to be able to approach is to be admitted into His presence.
H7132.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, always in a religious context. In Psalms 73:28, it expresses the supreme good for the believer: to draw near to God and trust Him. In Isaiah 58:2, it designates the desire that people have to meet God and know His justice. In both cases, the approach to God is presented as a voluntary act, a movement of the heart towards the Lord, rather than a mere external observance.
H7132.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that faith is primarily a personal drawing near to God. It is not a religion of distant laws and rituals, but a relationship of intimacy. Jesus made this approach possible for all by removing what separated us. It is an invitation to actively seek this closeness with the Lord in prayer and trust.

sens: Material gift presented to God during worship
Animal sacrifice offered to the Lord
Grain or incense oblation
Gift brought to honor God
H7133A.detail: 1. The offering is the material gift that a believer brings to the sanctuary to approach God and pay Him homage. In Leviticus 1:2, God commands Moses to tell the Israelites: "When anyone among you brings an offering to the Lord, he shall offer from the herd"—the offering is thus the very act of presenting something precious. 2. The offering often takes the form of a flawless animal sacrifice: a bull, a ram, a goat, or even birds depending on the wealth of the believer (Leviticus 1:3, 1:10, 1:14). These victims mark the seriousness of the dedication to God. 3. The offering can also be of a plant nature, fine flour with oil and incense (Leviticus 2:1, 2:4), offered especially by those who could not bring an animal. 4. Some offerings aim at a specific purpose: to appease a legitimate jealousy (Numbers 5:15), to seal a Nazarite vow (Numbers 6:14), or to fulfill a recognition towards God (Leviticus 7:15). They thus carry a spiritual meaning that goes beyond the mere cultic act.
H7133A.origine: The Hebrew word קׇרְבָּן comes from the root קרב (qrb), which means "to approach". The offering is therefore what "brings" the believer closer to God, allowing him to bridge the distance between sinful humanity and the holy God. This link between the offering and the approach is found in the name of the tabernacle itself, the place where the people could approach God. The family of this word includes the verb "to approach" and the noun "service" in the sanctuary.
H7133A.emploi: The word "offering" appears 76 times in the Old Testament, primarily in the books of Leviticus, Numbers, and Ezekiel. It first designates any cultic act of presentation to God (Leviticus 1:2), then the different categories: thanksgiving sacrifices, grain offerings, offerings from the princes for the dedication of the tabernacle (Numbers 7). In Ezekiel, the word also describes idolatrous offerings on the high places (Ezekiel 20:28), showing that the offering has value only if it is addressed to the true God with a right heart. The term thus covers all the sacrificial worship of the people of the Old Covenant.
H7133A.portee: The offering teaches the believer that approaching God costs something: it requires a gift, a renunciation, a personal loss. It also reminds us that everyone, poor or rich, can present themselves before the Lord with what they have. For the Christian, Jesus is the perfect offering who has definitively accomplished what all sacrifices foreshadowed, thus opening a permanent access to God without the need for sacrificial intermediaries.

sens: gift brought to God during worship
wood brought to the temple to fuel the altar
H7133B.detail:
1. An offering is a gift presented to God in worship, to honor Him or to atone for a fault. It is an act of devotion and respect towards the Lord. In Nehemiah 10:34, the Israelites commit to regularly bringing wood to the house of God: this wood is a material offering intended to keep the altar of sacrifices functioning.
2. More concretely in the context of the temple, the offering refers to the wood that was to be provided each year on fixed dates so that the fire could burn on the altar of the Lord. In Nehemiah 13:31, it is mentioned alongside the firstfruits (the first fruits of the harvest), showing that it was part of the regular religious obligations of the people towards God.
H7133B.origine: The word comes from the root meaning "to approach" or "to bring near": an offering is something that is brought near to God, presented before Him. This is a fundamental concept of Israelite worship, as it expresses the people's desire to stand close to God and to show Him their obedience. This root is found in other words related to sacrifices and religious acts.
H7133B.emploi: This word appears twice in the Bible, both times in the book of Nehemiah, at the heart of the story of the restoration of the temple and worship after the exile. In Nehemiah 10:34, it is during a great assembly where the people commit by oath to uphold God's law: they draw lots to determine who will bring the wood intended to be offered on the altar. In Nehemiah 13:31, Nehemiah reminds them of these commitments and asks God to remember his zeal for maintaining the offering of wood on its fixed dates. In these two verses, the offering has a very concrete and organized character: it is a collective responsibility, scheduled and distributed among families.
H7133B.portee: For the Christian reader, this notion of offering reminds us that serving God is not a matter of vague sentiment, but of regular and concrete commitment. The wood burned on the altar symbolizes the people's consecration to divine service: they give what they have so that worship can continue. This faithfulness in small things — providing the wood on fixed dates — reflects a stable and obedient piety that pleases God.

sens: sharp tool with a wide blade, mounted on a handle, used for chopping or splitting wood
blade of this tool, which can become dull or wear out
weapon or instrument of destruction used in war or for ravaging
H7134.detail:
1. The axe is a work tool consisting of a wide, sharp blade fixed to a handle, used for cutting wood. This is notably what Abimelech takes to make himself known to his companions: he cuts a branch from a tree with the axe to show his boldness (Judges 9:48). Israelite farmers regularly sharpened this tool, as shown by the enumeration of instruments they went down to sharpen among the Philistines (1 Samuel 13:20).
2. The blade of the axe, like any metal tool, dulls over time and with use. The text of 1 Samuel 13:21 speaks of sharpening again the "dull" edges — a term that expresses the gradual wear of the tool and the necessity of maintaining it.
3. The axe becomes an image of destructive force and power in war. Psalm 74:5 compares one who raises a hatchet in a thick forest to enemies ravaging the temple of God. Similarly, in Jeremiah 46:22, the Egyptian army advances "with axes, like lumberjacks" — an image that underscores the systematic and organized violence of the invasion.
H7134.origine: The Hebrew word קַרְדֹּם (qardom) literally denotes the axe, this ancient and universal tool for working wood. Its precise etymology remains uncertain, but it belongs to the concrete vocabulary of ancient Near Eastern tools. The word appears rarely in the biblical text (five occurrences), and it always imposes itself in contexts that highlight either utilitarian work or the image of destructive power.
H7134.emploi: The word appears five times in the Hebrew Bible, always in the singular. In 1 Samuel 13:20-21, it is listed among the agricultural tools that the Israelites had to have sharpened among the Philistines, a sign of Israel's technological dependence before its establishment. In Judges 9:48, the axe is a personal gesture of authority and courage. In later texts (Psalms 74:5 and Jeremiah 46:22), the axe becomes a powerful poetic figure: it represents the structured violence of the enemy, the methodical devastation, like the work of a lumberjack systematically felling trees. This progression from the concrete to the figurative shows how an ordinary tool can embody, in biblical language, the destructive force of judgment or conquest.
H7134.portee: The axe reminds us that God sees the instruments of our hands and our actions — those of honest work as well as those of destruction or domination. It also invites the reader to meditate on the power of God's word, often compared to a sharp weapon: just as an axe splits wood, so the Word divides the righteous from the unrighteous and reveals hearts. Finally, the images of axes raised against the people of God remind us that human power, however terrible, remains under the gaze and control of the Lord.

sens: The sensation of low temperature, the lack of warmth
The cold season, winter or its climatic effects
The physical discomfort caused by exposure to cold
The harshness, the severity of natural conditions
H7135.detail:
1. Cold is primarily the low temperature itself, what one feels when exposed to the elements without protection. Job 24:7 shows this cruelly: poor men spend the night naked, without clothing or covering "against the cold," exposed to the physical trial of the dropping temperature.
2. The word also refers to the cold season, winter with its difficult living conditions. In Job 37:9, cold comes "from the north winds," it is a massive climatic force that accompanies the storm. It is the power of winter that arises.
3. More broadly, cold evokes the harshness of natural trials. Psalm 147:17 speaks of the ice that God sends "in pieces" and the cold that cannot be faced: it is a demonstration of the formidable power of nature. Proverbs 25:20 uses the image: "removing one's garment on a cold day" is an absurd act, and similarly, singing before a sad heart is inappropriate and cruel.
H7135.origine: The Hebrew word קָרָה (qarah) is related to the idea of coldness and low temperature. It comes from a root expressing cooling, and belongs to the family of words describing concrete natural and sensory phenomena. It is a simple and direct term from everyday language, without particular theological connotation at the outset.
H7135.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the Bible, almost exclusively in the wisdom books and the prophets. It is encountered in Job (twice: 24:7 and 37:9) where it illustrates the misery of the poor or the power of the storm. The Psalms show it as a manifestation of divine power (147:17). Proverbs uses it in a moral image: physical cold becomes the symbol of an inappropriate action (25:20). Nahum uses the word once (3:17) to speak of the "coldness" where the locusts settle. Through these uses, cold remains concrete and sensory, but it can illustrate human trials or the power of God.
H7135.portee: Cold in the Bible is never abstract: it is the real physical trial of the poor and the needy, as in Job 24:7. This invites the reader to feel God's justice towards those who suffer from lack. Cold also reminds us that nature itself obeys God and manifests His formidable power. For the believer, it is an invitation to compassion towards the poor and an awareness that God sees all suffering.

sens: To be in the presence of someone, whether planned or unplanned
To come to meet someone
To occur, to happen, to take place
To be present by chance, to find oneself by luck
H7136A.detail:
1. To be in the presence of someone, whether planned or unplanned: this is the primary meaning of the word, which describes a meeting. Abraham's servant asks: "Let me meet the one you have appointed for your servant" (Genesis 24:12) — it refers to crossing paths with someone. God also says that He "came to meet Balaam" (Numbers 23:4), which shows a face-to-face presence.
2. To come to meet someone: this is a directed meeting, where one goes towards someone who may or may not be waiting. During Moses' vision, God "showed Himself" (or literally "came") to him at Sinai (Exodus 3:18).
3. To occur, to happen, to take place: the meaning broadens beyond meeting people to what "happens", what takes place. When Joseph tells his brothers: "Here is what has happened to me" (Genesis 42:29), he speaks of events that have occurred. Haman recounts "all that had happened to him" (Esther 6:13) — his misfortunes.
4. To be present by chance, to find oneself by luck: Ruth "happened to find herself" (Ruth 2:3) in Boaz's field — a fortuitous, unplanned meeting.
H7136A.origine: The verb הָרָק (qara) comes from a root that primarily evokes "meeting" in the sense of a convergence, of paths crossing. The root carries the image of two things colliding or meeting. The word gradually expands from "meeting someone" to "arriving, occurring", because events "happen" in our lives as encounters with destiny or with God. It is a very vivid, concrete verb, rooted in human experience.
H7136A.emploi: This verb appears 22 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the narratives of the Pentateuch (Genesis, Exodus, Numbers) and in the historical books. In the sense of "meeting", it describes factual encounters (Abraham's servant and Rebekah, God and Balaam) or the appearance of God. In the sense of "arriving, occurring", it is very frequent: it designates what happens to us, whether happy or unfortunate — a misfortune that occurs, an event that takes place. In Ecclesiastes (2:14, 2:15, 9:11), the author uses it to speak of the fate that befalls everyone, both the righteous and the wicked. The meaning thus refines: from the concrete (meeting a person) to the abstract (an event that happens), reflecting how the Bible intertwines the personal and divine providence.
H7136A.portee: This word invites the reader to see their life as a series of "meetings" — not only with others but with God and with events. It suggests that nothing happens to us by pure chance: every meeting, every circumstance is an opportunity to encounter the presence and intention of God. For the believer, becoming aware of these meetings is to recognize divine guidance in the details of their existence.

sens: Structure of beams or wood that forms the framework of a building
To cover or close an opening with a wooden structure
To build or form something by organizing its parts
To shape or mold
Arrangement or organization of elements
H7136B.detail:
1. Structure of beams or wood that forms the framework of a building — This is the set of woods that support and structure a building. In Jerusalem, when the Temple was being restored, wood was purchased "for the beams and framework of the buildings that the kings of Judah had destroyed" (2 Chronicles 34:11), and Nehemiah requested "timber for the framework of the gates of the citadel" (Nehemiah 2:8).
2. To cover or close an opening with a wooden structure — This is assembling wooden elements to form a functional door or gate. The fish gate and the old gate of Jerusalem were "covered": they were given their structure of leaves and bars (Nehemiah 3:3, 3:6).
3. To build or form something by organizing its parts — The word evokes the action of putting in place, composing. God "forms with the waters the roof of His dwelling" (Psalms 104:3): He organizes, He structures everything according to His plan.
H7136B.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of "to place" or "to set down". The primary meaning is very concrete: to arrange beams or woods one on top of the other to make the framework of a house. In the biblical context, it always involves an action of construction or composition with intention.
H7136B.emploi: This verb appears 5 times in the Hebrew Bible. Twice in 2 Chronicles and Nehemiah, it specifically refers to the framework of buildings and gates that are being rebuilt after devastation (2 Chronicles 34:11, Nehemiah 2:8, 3:3, 3:6). Once, it is used in the broader sense of "to form" or "to organize": God forms (structures) the heavens "with the waters" (Psalms 104:3). The word remains attached to the idea of organized composition, whether material (framework of stone and wood) or cosmic (the order of the heavens).
H7136B.portee: This word reminds us that all construction — whether spiritual, social, or material — rests on a solid framework, on well-assembled foundations. For the believer, it is an image of the necessity of order, structure, and organization in life. God Himself is presented as the one who "forms" the cosmos: there is wisdom and intention behind all creation.

sens: An unexpected and fortuitous event that happens to someone
Involuntary nocturnal pollution
H7137.detail:
1. An event that occurs by chance, without intention, in an unexpected manner. It is what happens without being planned or provoked — a fortuitous occurrence. In Deuteronomy 23:10, it specifically refers to an involuntary nocturnal pollution: a bodily event that occurs during sleep, outside the will of the one affected.
2. In the context of Levitical law, this accident temporarily renders the affected person impure. The person must leave the camp until evening (after having washed). It is not a moral fault, but a physical reality that requires cultic purification — the accident is a natural, non-blameworthy event, but it has ritual consequences in the life of God's people.
H7137.origine: The Hebrew word קָרֶה (qareh) comes from a root that means "to meet" or "to come to". It fundamentally designates what happens, what comes to meet someone, without their control. The central idea is that of the unexpected, the fortuitous — what "falls upon" someone rather than being deliberately provoked. The word evokes an occurrence that happens independently of one's will.
H7137.emploi: This word appears only once in Deuteronomy 23:10, in a very specific legislative context concerning the ritual purity of the camp. Moses states a law of purification: if a man experiences an involuntary nocturnal pollution, this "accident" temporarily renders him impure. He must leave the camp, wash, and remain outside until sunset, at which point he can re-enter the camp. This unique usage shows that the word designates a fortuitous event, without guilt, but which nonetheless has concrete cultic repercussions.
H7137.portee: This passage teaches that even the most ordinary and involuntary bodily realities are taken into account in life with God. It shows that purification is not a punishment for guilt, but a measure of order and holiness for the camp. For the believer, this illustrates that God governs all aspects of communal life, and that ritual impurity — here involuntary — requires a concrete restoration of the relationship with the holy community.

sens: Who is a short distance away in space
Who is not far away in time, imminent
Who belongs to the family, who is a relative
Who is present in the mind, whom one feels close to
H7138.detail:
1. This word primarily denotes physical proximity: that which is located at a short distance, as opposed to that which is distant. In Genesis 19:20, Lot asks for refuge in a city "near," not too far away for him to flee quickly. It can also express spatial immediacy, as in Ezekiel 22:5 where "those who are near" are contrasted with distant spectators.
2. The word then applies to temporal proximity, to that which is about to happen. In Joel 1:15, the day of the Lord is "near," announcing an imminent event. In Isaiah 55:6, seeking the Lord "while he is near" evokes an opportunity that will not last, a limited time.
3. It describes the relationship of kinship: a "near relative" is a family member. In Leviticus 21:2, the priest may become unclean for his near relatives, his true blood relations. Ruth 3:12 mentions a relative capable of redeeming property according to the law.
4. Finally, it expresses what is present in the mind or heart, that which one cannot escape. In 1 Kings 8:59, the king asks that his prayers remain "present" day and night before the Lord, meaning constantly in His attention.
H7138.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root that fundamentally means "to be near, to approach." The same family produces the verb "qārab" (to approach, to offer a sacrifice) and the noun "qōrāb" (offering). The image is one of reducing distance, whether spatial, temporal, or relational. The notion of offering comes from the idea of "bringing near" something to God, placing it in His presence.
H7138.emploi: This word is extremely frequent in the Hebrew Bible (75 documented uses), particularly in the Psalms and the prophets. In the Pentateuch, it mainly expresses kinship (Leviticus 21:2-3) and physical proximity. The psalmists use it to evoke the presence of God: "The Lord is near to those who call on him" (Psalms 145:18). The prophets use it to announce the imminence of divine judgment: "The day of the Lord is near" (Joel 1:15, Zephaniah 1:14). The affectionate or legal context (right of redemption, family obligations) shows that "near" can mean more than just a simple distance: it describes a responsibility or intimacy.
H7138.portee: This word reminds us that God is not distant or inaccessible. When Scripture affirms that the Lord is "near to those who call on him," it assures us of a real and benevolent presence. The idea of temporal urgency (the day of the Lord approaching) invites vigilance and conversion. Finally, the use of the word to describe kinship emphasizes that God's love for His people is a familial love, personal and committed.

sens: To remove the hair from the head by cutting it close
To have a bald or shaved head
To shave the head as a sign of mourning or distress
H7139.detail:
1. To shave the head means to completely remove the hair by cutting it very short. It is a concrete and visible action. In Ezekiel 29:18, after a long siege of Tyre, the soldiers of Nebuchadnezzar have "all bald heads," so exhausting was the effort.

2. Having a bald or shaved head can result from this action, or be a natural condition. This was remarkable in the Old Testament, where long hair was the norm, as shown in Leviticus 21:5 which forbids priests from "making a bald spot on their heads."

3. To shave the head was primarily a gesture of mourning, desolation, or humiliation in the face of a grave misfortune. In Ezekiel 27:31, the inhabitants of Tyre "will shave their heads" while mourning the destruction of their city, thus expressing their extreme affliction.
H7139.origine: The verb comes from a root that evokes nudity and absence. In Hebrew, baldness was often a visible sign of suffering or rupture — hence its use in mourning rites. The word is related to the general idea of stripping away or laying bare.
H7139.emploi: This verb appears about ten times in the Hebrew Bible. It has two main meanings. First, a literal sense: the priests in Israel were not to shave their heads (Leviticus 21:5), as it would have been an act of mourning incompatible with their service in the temple. Second, a ritual and emotional sense: shaving the head expressed deep sorrow or despair in the face of catastrophe. Thus, the Tyrians mourn their destroyed city (Ezekiel 27:31), and in Jeremiah 16:6, the people will be struck by such desolation that they will not even be able to perform this funeral rite. The absence of shaving then becomes a sign of even greater misfortune.
H7139.portee: This word reminds us that in the Old Testament, the body was the language of the heart. A gesture as visible as shaving the head expressed what words would struggle to convey: mourning, contrition, collapse. This helps us better understand the depth of emotions in the Psalms and Lamentations, and the place of the whole body — not just the soul — in the relationship with God.

sens: Intense frost or ice crystals formed by cold
Extreme cold of the night
Hard and frozen substance that obstructs or blocks the flow of water
H7140.detail:
1. Ice refers to natural frost or ice crystals formed when water freezes due to intense cold. In the book of Job, God produces ice and restrains the space where waters spread (Job 37:10): it is a force created by God Himself, and in the Psalms, the Lord sends forth His ice in pieces, so powerful that no one can withstand His cold (Psalms 147:17).
2. The winter or nighttime cold, when the temperature drops drastically. Jacob confesses that he endured the cold at night, while the heat consumed him during the day (Genesis 31:40); the corpse of Jehoiakim will be exposed to heat by day and cold by night (Jeremiah 36:30).
3. Ice chunks or debris that obstruct or disturb the flow of waters. Job describes the ice that troubles the course of rivers when snow rushes into them (Job 6:16): the image is one of water frozen, become solid and unnavigable.
H7140.origine: The Hebrew word qerach comes from a root expressing the idea of hardness and freezing. It literally denotes that which is hardened by cold. The word appears mainly in the poetic and wisdom books (Job, Psalms) where it evokes the creative and fearsome power of God over natural elements.
H7140.emploi: The word appears seven times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in the wisdom and poetry books (Job, Psalms, Jeremiah) and once in Ezekiel. In these texts, ice is never simply a neutral meteorological observation: it is either a human trial (the cold that Jacob endures) or a manifestation of God's power and majesty (God produces ice, God sends it forth in pieces). Genesis 31:40 shows ice as deprivation and suffering; Job 37:10 and Psalms 147:17 present it as a marvel of divine creation.
H7140.portee: Ice in the Bible symbolizes both the natural adversity that humans must face and the sovereign power of God over all creation. It reminds us that the forces of nature are not neutral or chaotic: they reveal the hand of the Creator and His majesty. For the reader, meditating on these verses invites recognition of God in the natural elements and trust in Him amid trials.

sens: Son of Esau and Oholibamah, chief of the Edomites during the patriarchal period
H7141G.detail: Koré is one of the sons of Esau born to his wife Oholibamah. He is mentioned several times in the genealogy of the Edomites as one of the chiefs (or "dukes") descended from Esau. His brothers, born of the same mother, are Jeush and Jalam (Genesis 36:5 and 36:14). The Bible places him among the descendants of Esau who gave rise to the peoples of Edom, and his name regularly appears in the genealogical lists tracing the lineage of Edomite chiefs (Genesis 36:18; 1 Chronicles 1:35).
H7141G.origine: The name Koré means "bald" in Hebrew, possibly evoking a physical characteristic. It is a name borne by several biblical characters, but this one specifically is the son of Esau, the brother of Jacob, and represents a branch of the Edomite family, the descendants of Esau who settled in the region of Edom.
H7141G.emploi: Koré appears only four times in the Bible, always in genealogical lists of the descendants of Esau. Two occurrences are found in Genesis 36, in verses 5 and 14, which enumerate his births. In verse 18 of the same chapter, he is designated as a chief or duke of Edom, confirming his importance in the structuring of this people. A fourth mention is found in 1 Chronicles 1:35, which repeats this same genealogy. Koré thus represents a royal or aristocratic lineage among the Edomites, the cousins of Israel.

sens: Son of Eliphaz and grandson of Esau, Edomite chief during the Patriarchs' time
H7141H.detail: Koré is a proper name referring to a man of the Edomite people. He is the son of Eliphaz and the grandson of Esau, and lived during the time of the Patriarchs. He is mentioned in Genesis 36:16 as one of the chiefs descended from Eliphaz in the land of Edom, alongside his brothers Gaetham and Amalek.
H7141H.origine: The name Koré means "bald" in Hebrew, possibly evoking a physical characteristic of this Edomite ancestor. It is a Semitic patronymic borne by several characters in the Bible, but it specifically refers here to this Edomite chief, distinct from other namesakes.
H7141H.emploi: Koré is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Genesis 36:16, in the genealogy of the descendants of Esau. This passage lists the Edomite chiefs descended from Eliphaz and his wives, thus establishing the list of powers that ruled over Edom in the early days of the Hebrew people. His appearance fits within the context of genealogical lists tracing the origins of the neighboring peoples of Israel.

sens: A Levite during the Exodus and the wilderness, leader of a revolt against Moses and Aaron
Descendant of Levi through the line of Kohath and Izhar
Father of several sons, some of whom become temple musicians
One of the dukes of Edom, son of Esau
H7141I.detail:
1. Koré is a Levite who lived during the time of the Exodus and the wilderness. He is the son of Izhar, himself the son of Kohath and grandson of Levi (Exodus 6:21). He becomes famous for organizing a great revolt against Moses and Aaron, contesting their authority and that of the priesthood (Numbers 16:1-3). This rebellion ends tragically: the earth opens under Koré and his household, and fire from heaven consumes them (Numbers 16:32).
2. Despite Koré's death, not all of his descendants perish: "The sons of Koré did not die" (Numbers 26:11). His descendants play an important role in the temple of Jerusalem, notably as gatekeepers and musicians (1 Chronicles 9:19).
3. The sons of Koré are associated with the composition of several psalms: at least ten psalms bear his name or that of his descendants, including Psalms 42, 44, 45, 46, 47, 48, 49, 84, 85, 87, and 88. These psalms were composed by his descendants and are part of the temple worship songs.
H7141I.origine: The name "Koré" means "bald" in Hebrew. Koré was a cousin of Moses and Aaron, as he descended from the same Levitical family. His grandfather Kohath and that of Moses were brothers, both sons of Levi. The Bible also mentions other Korés: a son of Eliphaz (himself a son of Esau) and a son of Esau directly, both dukes of Edom.
H7141I.emploi: Koré is mentioned 31 times in the Bible, primarily in the book of Numbers. He first appears in the genealogy of the Exodus (Exodus 6:21), then becomes the center of a major crisis in Numbers 16. The revolt of Koré is one of the founding events of the Old Testament, illustrating divine judgment against pride and the challenge to authority established by God. After his death, his descendants remain significant: they are found as temple keepers (1 Chronicles 9:19) and as composers or singers associated with many psalms. These psalms of the sons of Koré constitute a collection of prayers and songs that span the entire history of Israel.
H7141I.portee: The story of Koré teaches that rebellion against the order established by God leads to judgment, but also that God's grace surpasses sin: the descendants of Koré, instead of disappearing, become servants of worship and authors of psalms that express the prayer of Israel. For the reader, this is a reminder of the importance of humility before the authority that God establishes, and an illustration of how God can transform the descendants of rebels into instruments of His praise.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah during the divided monarchy
H7141J.detail: 1. Koré is a man belonging to the tribe of Judah, mentioned only once in the Bible. He lived during the time when the kingdom of Israel was divided into two rival kingdoms (after the death of Solomon). He was the son of Hebron and brother of Thappuah, Rekem, and Shema (1 Chronicles 2:43). Few details are given about his life or actions.
H7141J.origine: The name Koré means "bald" in Hebrew. It is a descriptive name that likely refers to a distinctive physical trait. Although this same name is borne by other more famous biblical characters (notably Koré the Levite who rebelled against Moses in the wilderness), this Koré is a different person, simply a descendant of Hebron in the genealogy of Judah.
H7141J.emploi: This man is mentioned only in the genealogical list of the clan of Hebron in 1 Chronicles 2:43. He appears as the eldest of the four sons of Hebron, alongside his three brothers Thappuah, Rekem, and Shema. No account or particular action is reported about him; he is cited only to establish the genealogical lineage of Judah.

sens: Devoid of hair on the head
Who has lost their hair due to illness or age
H7142.detail:
1. In the simplest and most concrete sense, a bald man is one who has no hair on his head. In ancient Israel, this could result from a skin disease: in Leviticus 13:40, the diagnosis regarding leprosy (tsara'at) specifies that "when a man has a bald head, he is clean" — in other words, if baldness occurs without other symptoms of this contagious disease, the man is not unclean according to the Law. It is a medical sign that helps identify whether someone is ill or simply aging.
2. The word also refers to one who has lost their hair, whether naturally due to age or prematurely. In 2 Kings 2:23, children mock the prophet Elisha by shouting, "Get out of here, baldhead!" — an insult that plays on his physical appearance. This passage shows that baldness was noticeable and could serve as a subject of mockery.
H7142.origine: The Hebrew word קֵרֵחַ (qereach) expresses the idea of nakedness or deprivation: the head is "naked" of hair. The root evokes a smooth and exposed surface. This simple and descriptive term has no religious connotations in itself, but it is important for diagnosing skin diseases in Levitical legislation.
H7142.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, and only in these specific contexts. In Leviticus 13:40, it is found in the priestly prescriptions for diagnosing leprosy: it is an objective criterion for distinguishing between ritual impurity and simple baldness. In 2 Kings 2:23, the word becomes a narrative element: it characterizes Elisha and serves as a starting point for the mockery of the children. The term thus remains neutral in the first case (medical-legal diagnosis) and descriptive in the second (remarkable physical trait).
H7142.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible does not hide the reality of the human body and its transformations. In the legal context of Leviticus, it shows how the Law carefully distinguishes between the normal and the pathological, thus protecting the sick and gathering the community on clear criteria. In the narrative of 2 Kings, it also illustrates how physical appearances can become a pretext for mockery — a biblical wisdom invites respect for others beyond their visible traits.

sens: Father of Johanan and Jonathan, military leaders of Judah at the time of the destruction of the Southern Kingdom
H7143.detail: 1. Karéach is a Jewish military leader during the time of the ruin of Jerusalem and the Babylonian exile (around 586 B.C.). He is best known as the father of Johanan, who will play an important role after the assassination of Governor Gedaliah. He is first mentioned in the list of military commanders who submit to Gedaliah, appointed by the king of Babylon to administer the territory (2 Kings 25:23). Johanan, his son, becomes a central figure in the events that follow: he warns Gedaliah of Ishmael's plot (Jeremiah 40:16), then avenges the murder of this governor by catching Ishmael and freeing the prisoners (Jeremiah 41:16). The name Karéach means "bald" and thus refers to a physically bald man.
H7143.origine: The Hebrew name קָרֵחַ comes from a root that means to be bald or shaven. It is a physical characteristic given as a proper name, as was done in biblical antiquity. The literal meaning "bald" only appears as a personal name: it is a distinguishing trait used to identify the man among his peers.
H7143.emploi: Karéach appears only as the father of Johanan and Jonathan in the accounts of the fall of Jerusalem and the governorship of Gedaliah. The fourteen occurrences of the name in the Bible are all concentrated around the events of 2 Kings 25:23 and the book of Jeremiah (chapters 40-43). Johanan, son of Karéach, is featured as the most active and loyal military leader: he defends Gedaliah, avenges his death, and later seeks to consult the prophet Jeremiah before deciding the future of what remains of the Judean people. Karéach himself never intervenes directly: he is named only to identify his illustrious son.
H7143.portee: Karéach reminds us that even in the darkest moments — the destruction of the kingdom, the exile — God raises faithful men to protect His people. His son Johanan embodies this faithfulness: he refuses crime, protects the innocent, and seeks God's will through the prophet. It is a call to loyalty to God and to one another, even when everything is collapsing.

sens: absence of hair on the head, state of one who is bald
shaved area or part of the head devoid of hair
sign of mourning or sorrow: shaving the head in lamentation
mark of shame or curse
state of nakedness or deprivation
H7144.detail:
1. Baldness literally refers to the absence of hair on the head, whether natural or induced. This is what is called being bald or having a bald head (Isaiah 3:24).
2. The word also specifically refers to an intentionally shaved area: a part of the head from which hair has been cut. The priests of Israel were to abstain from this religious practice (Leviticus 21:5).
3. In Israel, shaving the head was an act of intense mourning, affliction, or lamentation in the face of death or misfortune. People would completely shave their heads and strike their chests as a sign of deep sorrow (Isaiah 22:12: "you shall shave your heads and put on sackcloth").
4. Baldness can also signify humiliation, shame, or a curse sent by God. Moab will lose its beauty and bear the mark of its defeat (Jeremiah 47:5: "Gaza has become bald").
5. In a broader image, baldness evokes deprivation and nakedness: what was covered with glory (the hair, a symbol of beauty) is suddenly exposed and diminished.
H7144.origine: The Hebrew word קׇרְחָה (qorkhah) comes from the root קרח which etymologically means "to be smooth, polished." The bald skull is indeed smooth, devoid of the covering of hair. This root thus evokes the idea of nakedness or exposure. Words of the same family describe other forms of nakedness or smoothness. The word expresses the image of a surface cleared, without protection or ornament.
H7144.emploi: The word appears about 11 times in the Old Testament, especially among the prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel) and in the laws (Leviticus, Deuteronomy). In Moses, it refers to a practice forbidden to the Israelites: shaving a bald spot was a pagan rite of mourning or magic that was to be rejected (Leviticus 21:5; Deuteronomy 14:1). Among the prophets, the word takes on a dimension of punishment or affliction: enemy peoples (Moab, Gaza) will see their heads become bald as a sign of their defeat, and the Israelites will shave their heads as a gesture of repentance and lamentation in the face of divine judgment (Isaiah 22:12; Jeremiah 48:37; Ezekiel 7:18). The context varies from religious rite to manifestation of mourning or judgment.
H7144.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that the outer body expresses the inner state: mourning is visibly manifested, and the nakedness or deprivation of the head signals a loss, humiliation, or transformation. It also shows that God wants His people to stand out: the Israelites were not to imitate pagan mourning rites (shaving the head), for their identity was in Him alone, not in outward gestures. Finally, baldness can remind us of the fragility of human beauty in the face of divine judgment.

sens: Descendant de Korah, qui était un lévite du temps de l'Égypte et du désert
Membre de la tribu ou du clan des descendants de Korah
H7145.detail:
1. A Korahite is a descendant of Korah, a Levite mentioned for the first time at the time of the Exodus from Egypt (Exodus 6:21). Korah was the son of Izhar and the brother of Nepheg, Zichri, and Shelomith. His sons — Assir, Elkana, and Abiasaph — founded the Korahite families that continued in Israel (Exodus 6:24).
2. The Korahites formed a distinctive clan among the Levites. They performed religious and official functions in the tabernacle and the temple, notably as gatekeepers and guardians of the thresholds of the tent of the Lord (1 Chronicles 9:19). Several of them are specifically mentioned in the records of the Church of Israel, such as Meshelemiah and his sons who kept the entrance of the temple (1 Chronicles 26:1).
H7145.origine: The term "Korahite" comes from the proper name Korah (קֹ֫רַח), a Levite from the time of the desert, and literally means "one who belongs to Korah" or "descendant of Korah." It is formed by the Hebrew gentilic adjective that denotes belonging to a clan or family lineage. Korah himself was a Levite from the branch of Amram.
H7145.emploi: The term "Korahite" appears eight times in the Bible, primarily in Chronicles, where it specifically refers to the descendants of the Korah clan among the Levites. Exodus 6:24 lists the three sons of Korah and identifies their descendants as "Korahites." Numbers 26:58 mentions the "family of the Korahites" among the Levitical families. In the accounts of Chronicles, the Korahites appear as temple gatekeepers (1 Chronicles 9:19, 26:1) and participants in religious services (1 Chronicles 12:6, 2 Chronicles 20:19). Their name thus persists throughout the history of Israel as a distinct Levitical clan with specific cultic responsibilities.
H7145.portee: The Korahites remind us that serving God within His people passes through established lineages and communities, and that even generations apart from one's ancestor, the call to service persists. Their faithfulness in the tasks entrusted to them — guarding the thresholds of the sanctuary — shows that an apparently simple duty gains its dignity in the service rendered to God.

sens: Zone du cuir chevelu dépourvue de cheveux
Endroit chauve, qu'il soit naturel ou causé par une maladie
Surface de peau atteinte par une plaie ou une affection (lèpre)
H7146.detail:
1. Baldness primarily refers to an area of the head where hair has disappeared. It can be natural (aging) or pathological. In Leviticus 13:42, the text speaks of the "bald part in front or behind" the head, areas where hair is normally or abnormally absent.

2. The term applies to any bald area of the body, whether the result of time or disease. Leviticus 13:43 mentions how to examine a "bald part in back or front" for signs of leprosy: it is on this exposed surface that a "tumor of a reddish-white sore" appears.

3. By extension, the term designates any skin surface that is eroded or damaged by an affliction. In Leviticus 13:55, it refers to the "part" or "place" that has been "eroded": baldness here becomes an image of skin stripped of its normal protection.
H7146.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to scratch" or "to make disappear." Baldness is conceived as a surface where something has been removed or destroyed. This root evokes the idea of bareness: what was covered has become bare and visible. This is why the term also applies to wounds or skin lesions that leave the skin exposed.
H7146.emploi: The term appears only three times in the Bible, all in Leviticus 13, at the heart of the laws concerning skin diseases and leprosy. It is a medical or administrative term: the priest must examine the "bald part" for signs of leprosy (a reddish-white sore, tumor). The context shows that natural baldness or that due to age was not considered a ritual impurity; however, if a suspicious skin lesion appeared, it indicated a contagious and serious disease. The term thus becomes an anatomical marker for diagnosis.
H7146.portee: This entry reminds the reader that the Old Testament placed great importance on bodily health and community hygiene. The laws regarding leprosy aimed to protect the people from a devastating disease. Seeing priests carefully examine each area of the body, including bald areas, shows the seriousness with which God treated physical purity and communal life in Israel.

sens: S'opposer à quelqu'un, lui faire face avec hostilité
Refuser d'obéir, rejeter une demande ou un ordre
Affronter quelqu'un en ennemi, lui résister activement
H7147.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the action of directly opposing someone, facing them as an adversary. It is a confrontation where one opposes the other. In Leviticus 26:24, God says: "I will also resist you," meaning that God Himself will stand against Israel as an enemy who opposes them.
2. The word also expresses the refusal to obey, particularly the refusal to listen to or follow an order. In Leviticus 26:21, God says to Israel: "If you resist me and do not want to listen," which shows that resisting God is to refuse to accept His words and commandments.
3. More broadly, it is an active hostility, a confrontation where the one who resists deliberately places themselves in opposition. In Leviticus 26:40, it speaks of "the resistance they have opposed to me," referring to the entirety of the rebellion and insubordination of the people towards God.
H7147.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of meeting someone face to face, but with a nuance of opposition and conflict. The image is that of two forces colliding: they meet, but as enemies. The root carries within it the idea of confrontation, of direct and hostile opposition.
H7147.emploi: This word appears 7 times in the Bible, almost exclusively in Leviticus, chapter 26, where God outlines the consequences of Israel's unfaithfulness. The word recurs six times throughout verses 21, 23, 24, 27, 28: God announces that He will strike Israel seven times more if the people "resist" and refuse to obey. A seventh occurrence in Leviticus 26:40 transfers it to the noun: "the resistance they have opposed to me." The word is thus clearly associated with the voluntary disobedience of the people towards God and the confrontation that results from it.
H7147.portee: This word reminds us that refusing to listen to God is to stand against Him as His adversary. There is no neutral position: one who does not obey God opposes Him. It is a warning that invites submission and obedience, showing that rebellion places the believer in direct confrontation with God Himself.

sens: To call someone to come to an assembly
To be summoned, called to participate in a meeting
To have the status of a recognized member of a community
H7148.detail:
1. To summon means to officially call someone to present themselves at an assembly or meeting. It is an act of authority that gathers people to deliberate together. In Numbers 16:2, the rebels against Moses are described as "those who were summoned to the assembly": these are men who were regularly called to the people's meetings, recognized and influential figures.
2. To be summoned means to receive this call and to be expected at the assembly. This term refers less to the act of summoning than to the status of the one who is the object of it: the one who "is summoned" to the assembly is a legally recognized and heard member. In Numbers 26:9, the same term qualifies Dathan and Abiram: they held this status of prominent individuals called to participate in the affairs of the people.
3. By extension, it means to have a recognized place or role in the community. The verb expresses less a one-time invitation than belonging to a circle of advisors or representatives who are regularly called upon.
H7148.origine: The Hebrew root expresses the idea of calling, crying out to someone. The word קָרִיא (qarî) is an adjective or participle meaning literally "the one who is called" or "called." It comes from the verb קָרָא (qara) whose fundamental meaning is "to cry out, to call." In biblical Hebrew, this root covers direct calling (crying out someone's name), invocation (calling on God), summoning (calling an assembly), and even proclamation (publicly calling out news). The word belongs to the same semantic field as its derivatives: מִקְרָא (miqra, "the summoned assembly").
H7148.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Old Testament, both times in relation to Korah's rebellion against Moses. In Numbers 16:2, it qualifies the two hundred fifty prominent men who rose up against Moses: they are "those who were summoned to the assembly," meaning recognized dignitaries of the people. In Numbers 26:9, the same term applies to Dathan and Abiram, two of the leaders of this rebellion. The context emphasizes: these men had an official status, they were not anonymous, but figures of authority who were consulted. The tragic irony of the narrative is that these prominent men, regularly summoned to assemblies, revolted against the order established by Moses and God.
H7148.portee: This word reminds us that every position of responsibility or influence among God's people comes from a calling, a summoning. The men who held a place of honor in the assembly of Israel received it from God, not earned it themselves. The fate of Dathan, Abiram, and the other rebels shows the danger of pride: one who feels called, honored, may revolt and be lost. It is a lesson for anyone who receives a responsibility: it is a gift, not a possession, and it requires obedience to God.

sens: Urban agglomeration with its walls, inhabitants, and structures
Fortified entity capable of revolting or refusing obedience
Center of power and political and fiscal stakes
H7149.detail:
1. The word designates a city as an organized human agglomeration, particularly with its walls and defenses. In the context of letters sent to the king of Persia, it refers to Jerusalem: a city rebuilt with its walls raised (Ezra 4:12, 4:15).

2. A city can be characterized by its political behavior: "rebellious and wicked" or seditious. The word then evokes not only the building but the community that inhabits it and its propensity for revolt (Ezra 4:15, 4:19).

3. A city is also a stake of power and royal taxation. Its reconstruction threatens the king's control and revenues: if its walls are raised, the king will lose "possession" of that region (Ezra 4:16). The word thus designates a strategic political center.
H7149.origine: The Hebrew word קִרְיָה (qir.yah) comes from a root that refers to the idea of calling, clamor, or gathering, but it has specialized to designate the city itself. It is related to קָרָא (qara, to call): a city is a place where voices intersect, where people gather. It is a common term for "city" or "town" in biblical Hebrew and the rest of the ancient Near East.
H7149.emploi: The word appears 7 times in the Bible, exclusively in Ezra 4, where it designates Jerusalem through the accusations that the adversaries of the Jews address to the king of Persia. The term recurs 6 times in the passage Ezra 4:10-21 to hammer home an argument: this city has always been rebellious, it threatens royal order, and its reconstruction constitutes insubordination. The word is used in an administrative and diplomatic context, not narrative: it aims to persuade the king that the city in question is a hotbed of trouble. The repetition of the term creates a rhetoric of alert and legitimization of the royal refusal.
H7149.portee: This word reminds us that the walls and urban structures are never neutral: they embody the power, autonomy, and capacity for resistance of a people. For the Christian reader, it illustrates how the People of God must confront the opposition of the world: the reconstruction of Jerusalem threatens human authorities. The word invites us to see that faithfulness to God inevitably provokes suspicion and hostility from the powers of the age.

sens: Action of proclaiming, announcing a message or order publicly
Message proclaimed, word widely disseminated
Official announcement intended to be heard by the people
H7150.detail:
1. The word designates the action of proclaiming, that is, announcing something aloud in a public and solemn manner. It is more than a simple word: it is a cry that is heard, a call made for all to listen. When Jonah is to make a "publication" in Nineveh, he is not sent to speak in secret, but to proclaim a message of repentance that the entire city must receive (Jonah 3:2).
2. By extension, the word can also refer to the message itself that is proclaimed — the word that is disseminated, the content of the announcement. It is what is published, what is made public.
3. The meaning can include the idea of an order or official directive that is made known to all, an announcement that carries weight of authority.
H7150.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root קָרָא (qara), which fundamentally means "to call" or "to cry out." This root evokes the image of a voice rising, projecting a sound far. The form קְרִיאָה is a noun derived from this root and retains its spirit well: it is the action of calling, crying out, and consequently announcing publicly.
H7150.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible: in Jonah 3:2, where the Lord commands Jonah to make a "publication" in Nineveh to announce His impending judgment. In this unique context, it is a prophetic announcement, a proclamation of divine judgment intended to call the inhabitants to repentance. The usage emphasizes the public and solemn nature of the message: it is not a whispered word, but a proclamation that must be heard by all.
H7150.portee: For the reader, this word reminds us of the importance of proclaiming the divine message. God does not hide His judgment or grace: He announces them publicly, so that everyone is confronted with reality and has the opportunity to respond. It is a call not to keep God's word to oneself, but to announce it frankly and widely, as Jonah was to do in Nineveh.

sens: Urban agglomeration with its inhabitants and structures
Center of political and administrative power
Fortified and protected place
Community organized as a collective entity
Image of strength and stability
Refuge or shelter
H7151.detail:
1. A city is an agglomeration of grouped dwellings with its inhabitants: this is the most direct meaning of the word. Numbers 21:28 speaks of "the city of Sihon" as a center from which a devastating fire springs forth, showing that the city represents the central home of a people.

2. It also embodies political power and authority: Isaiah 1:26 speaks of restoring "your judges" and calling Jerusalem "city of justice," revealing that the city is the seat of government and law.

3. The city is naturally fortified and protected by walls: Proverbs 18:11 compares wealth to "a strong city" and "a high wall," an image showing that the city symbolizes security and defense.

4. As a collective entity, the city can be personified or designated as a united community: Isaiah 25:3 evokes "the cities of the mighty nations," speaking of cities as historical actors with their own identity.

5. Finally, city can figuratively evoke anything that is stable, durable, and of great value: Isaiah 33:20 describes Zion, "city of our appointed feasts," as a place of stability where "the stakes will never be removed."

6. It sometimes becomes an image of refuge or trust: the strong city symbolizes where one finds shelter.
H7151.origine: The Hebrew word קִרְיָה (qiryah) comes from a root that likely means "to encircle" or "to delimit," expressing the idea of a clearly defined and inhabited space. This root reflects the very essence of a city: a circumscribed, protected place with boundaries. In Aramaic, the form is identical (קִרְיָה). In the Greek Old Testament, the corresponding Greek word is generally πόλις (polis), which carries the same meaning of an organized "city."
H7151.emploi: The word קִרְיָה (qiryah) appears 29 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in the historical and prophetic books. It first designates real cities as centers of habitation: Deuteronomy 2:36 and 3:4 speak of the "cities" conquered in Transjordan. But it also takes on a symbolic charge among the prophets: Isaiah uses it abundantly (at least 8 times) to evoke Jerusalem as the "city of justice" (Isaiah 1:26) or Jerusalem as a center of feasts (Isaiah 33:20). Proverbs uses it figuratively: "wealth is a strong city for the rich" (Proverbs 18:11). Among the judgment prophets (Jeremiah, Lamentations, Micah), the word takes on a tragic dimension, evoking destroyed cities. Job 39:10 uses it to emphasize that certain creatures do not care about the "tumult of cities."
H7151.portee: This word reminds us that the city is not just a simple geographical location, but embodies the order, government, justice, and culture of a people. The Bible often contrasts the just city with the corrupt city, inviting the reader to reflect on what they are building: a city of justice or a city of violence. Understanding that the city can be "strong" as an image of trust also invites us to examine what we truly place our assurance in: wealth, power, or the living God.

sens: City in the south of Judah
H7152G.detail: Carioth is a city located in the southern region of the territory of Judah. Its name means "the cities" in Hebrew, perhaps because it was a center grouping several small settlements or an important crossroads. It appears in the list of cities that Joshua assigns to the tribe of Judah during the division of the promised land.
H7152G.origine: The name Carioth comes from the Hebrew קְרִיּוֹת (qeriyot), which literally means "the cities" (plural of "city"). This plural form suggests a place where several villages were grouped or fortified together.
H7152G.emploi: Carioth appears only once in the Bible, in the list of cities assigned to Judah in Joshua 15:25. It was located in the south of Judah, among the cities of the Negev region, the southern desert. Its unique appearance in the territorial division lists indicates that it was an established locality, although few details have come down to us.

sens: City of Moab
Fortresses of Moab
Center of Moabite power
H7152H.detail: Kerijoth is an important city in the kingdom of Moab, located east of the Jordan. The name literally means "cities" in Hebrew, probably because it was either an agglomeration of several villages or a center grouping several sanctuaries or royal palaces. In the three passages where it appears, it is presented as a key place of Moabite power: in Jeremiah 48:24, it is listed among the great cities of the land; in Jeremiah 48:41, its capture is a decisive turning point in the conquest, symbolizing the collapse of the kingdom; in Amos 2:2, its palaces are marked for divine destruction, highlighting its role as the seat of royal or religious power.
H7152H.origine: The Hebrew word קְרִיּוֹת (qeriyot) is the plural of קִרְיָה (qiryah, "city"), formed from the root קור (qur) which evokes the idea of construction or foundation. The name thus evokes an "assembly of cities" or "fortified city." It is another designation for Kiriathaim, mentioned in Genesis 14:5 as a city of the Emims.
H7152H.emploi: Kerijoth appears three times in the Bible, all in the context of prophecies against Moab. Jeremiah speaks of it as one of the main cities of the land (48:24), then as a stronghold whose fall symbolizes the ruin of the entire kingdom (48:41). Amos mentions it to announce the destruction of its palaces by divine fire (2:2). These three passages date from the 8th-6th century B.C., a period of political instability in Moab. Kerijoth thus represents the administrative and military heart of the country, and its foretold destruction signifies the end of Moab as a political power.

sens: Ancient city of Canaan, located in the hill country of Judah
Former name of the city of Hebron
The city associated with Arba, a giant Anakim
Burial place of the patriarchs and matriarchs
H7153.detail:
1. Kirjath-Arba is an ancient city in the land of Canaan, established in the hill country of Judah. The name literally means "city of Arba." This is the name it bore before being called Hebron (Joshua 14:15).
2. It is the same city as Hebron, which became one of the three cities of refuge in Israel (Joshua 20:7). After the conquest, the name Hebron prevailed, although Kirjath-Arba is still used at times.
3. Its ancient name recalls Arba, a man who was the greatest among the Anakim, those giants of the land of Canaan (Joshua 14:15). That is why the city bore his name.
4. This city is famous in patriarchal history: it is at Kirjath-Arba (Hebron) that Sarah died, and Abraham came to mourn her (Genesis 23:2), and it is also where Jacob found his father Isaac (Genesis 35:27).
H7153.origine: The name "Kirjath-Arba" is composed of two Hebrew elements: "kirjath" (קִרְיַת), which means "city," and "Arba" (אַרְבַּע), the name of a giant Anakim from whom the city took its name. Arba was renowned for his great stature among the original inhabitants of Canaan. The name changed after the Israelite conquest, but biblical texts continue to mention the old name to clarify the identity of the city.
H7153.emploi: Kirjath-Arba appears nine times in the Bible, primarily in Genesis and the book of Joshua. It is first mentioned as the place where Sarah died (Genesis 23:2), then where Jacob found Isaac (Genesis 35:27). After the conquest of the land, the biblical text regularly specifies that Kirjath-Arba is the old name of Hebron (Joshua 14:15; 15:13; 20:7). The city was given to Caleb as an inheritance (Joshua 15:13) and became one of the three cities of refuge and a city for the Levites (Joshua 20:7).
