The old name reminds us that this city, although occupied by the Israelites, had a long history linked to the indigenous peoples of Canaan.

sens: City in Palestine located at the northern border of Judah and the western and southern borders of Benjamin
Old name of Kirjath-Jearim
H7154.detail:
1. Kirjath-Baal is a city situated at a crossroads of borders: it marks the northern limit of the territory of Judah and is also located on the western and southern boundaries of the territory of Benjamin. In Joshua 15:60, it is listed among the cities of Judah, and in Joshua 18:14, it delineates the western side of the Benjaminite territory. It is a strategic point of demarcation between the two tribes.
2. Kirjath-Baal and Kirjath-Jearim refer to the same place: both passages in Joshua explicitly state "Kirjath-Baal, which is Kirjath-Jearim." This dual name may reflect a religious history of the site, where the old name "Baal" (the Canaanite god) was replaced by "Jearim" ("of the forests"), marking the transition to the worship of the God of Israel.
H7154.origine: The name literally means "city of Baal": "Kirjath" (קִרְיַת) means "city" in Hebrew, and "Baal" (בַּעַל) is the name of the chief god of the Canaanite pantheon, worshiped in many places in the ancient Near East. This name bears witness to a Canaanite past of the site, before the Israelite conquest. The place was later designated by the name Kirjath-Jearim, which evokes the surrounding forests, showing how the name changed over time.
H7154.emploi: Kirjath-Baal appears twice in the Bible, only in the book of Joshua, in chapters 15 and 18. These two mentions are part of the lists of borders and land distribution among the tribes of Israel after the conquest. The city occupies a key position as a landmark for delineating the territories of Judah and Benjamin. The texts specify each time that this ancient name corresponds to Kirjath-Jearim, suggesting that the readers of the biblical text no longer recognized the ancient Canaanite name and needed clarification.
H7154.portee: This name reminds us that Palestine before Israel was inhabited by Canaanite peoples with their own gods and places of worship. The name change from Kirjath-Baal to Kirjath-Jearim symbolizes the transformation of the land and its integration into God's plan for His people. For the Christian reader, it is a sign that God reclaims a land dedicated to false gods and assigns it to His people according to His promises.

sens: City of Moab where King Balak welcomed the prophet Balaam
H7155.detail: Kirjath-Hutsoth is a city located in Moab, a region east of the Jordan. Its name literally means "city of streets" or "city of squares." It is where King Balak brought the prophet Balaam after summoning him to curse the people of Israel (Numbers 22:39).
H7155.origine: The name is composed of two Hebrew words: "kirya" (קִרְיָה), which means "city," and "hutsor" (חֻצוֹת), which refers to the streets or public squares of a city. It is a descriptive name that emphasizes the urban character of the place, perhaps a center of regional importance.
H7155.emploi: Kirjath-Hutsoth appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 22:39. It is mentioned as the place where Balak received Balaam after his journey from Mesopotamia. It is the starting point of the famous story where Balaam, supposed to curse Israel, instead blesses God's people three times, overturning the plans of the Moabite king.

sens: City of Moab, east of the Jordan
H7156G.detail: Kirjathaïm is a city located in Moabite territory, on the eastern bank of the Jordan. The name literally means "two cities," suggesting that it was originally composed of two settlements (Genesis 14:5; Numbers 32:37). It is mentioned among the cities that the sons of Reuben rebuilt after the conquest (Numbers 32:37), and it appears in the lists of Moabite cities, notably Joshua 13:19. In the oracles against Moab, the prophets Jeremiah and Ezekiel cite it as a symbol of the impending destruction upon this enemy people of Israel (Jeremiah 48:1; Ezekiel 25:9).
H7156G.origine: The Hebrew name קִרְיָתַיִם (Kirjathaïm) literally means "two cities": קִרְיָה (qiryah, "city") in the dual form. This formation suggests that the place included two distinct urban centers or two parts. Variants of the name exist: Shaveh-Kirjathaïm in Genesis 14:5 adds "Shaveh" ("plain"), and Kirjathaïm Misgab in Jeremiah 48:1 adds "Misgab" ("height"). Another name, Kerioth (קְרִיּוֹת), might refer to the same locality or a neighboring one.
H7156G.emploi: Kirjathaïm appears six times in the Hebrew Bible, always as a proper geographical name. It is first mentioned in the context of ancient warfare (Genesis 14:5, where it is already established), then as a city rebuilt by the tribe of Reuben after the conquest of Transjordan (Numbers 32:37) and listed in the borders of the territory of Judah in Joshua 13:19. However, it is primarily known through the prophetic oracles against Moab, in Jeremiah and Ezekiel, where it symbolizes the Moabite cities condemned to desolation for their hostility towards Israel. These references show that Kirjathaïm was an important and strategic city in the Moabite plateau.
H7156G.portee: Kirjathaïm reminds biblical readers that God's judgment extends to all nations and cities, not just Israel. It illustrates how the Lord controls the history of neighboring peoples and executes His plans of justice on those who oppose His people. It is a call to trust in divine sovereignty over global events.

sens: City of the tribe of Naphtali in Israel
Place assigned to the Gershonite Levites
H7156I.detail:
1. Kirjathaïm is a city located in the territory of the tribe of Naphtali, in northern Galilee. Its name means "two cities" in Hebrew, suggesting that it was composed of two nearby or administratively united localities. In the context of 1 Chronicles 6:76, it is listed among the cities with their pasture lands.
2. This city was specifically assigned to the Levites descended from Gershon, that is, to a class of priests responsible for the service of the tabernacle and the temple. Kirjathaïm was thus among the cities of refuge and habitation reserved for the servants of divine worship in Israel.
H7156I.origine: The Hebrew name קִרְיָתַיִם (qir'yatayim) is composed of קִרְיָה (qir'yah, "city") and the dual תַיִם (tayim, "two"), literally "two cities." This formation reflects the geography of the place: probably two distinct settlements treated as a single administrative entity. The word קִרְיָה appears in many biblical city names (Qiryat-Arba, Qiryat-Yéarim, etc.).
H7156I.emploi: Kirjathaïm appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 6:76, in the list of Levitical cities distributed to the clans of priests after the conquest of Canaan. It is mentioned alongside Kedesh in Galilee and Hammon, all three with their surrounding lands designated for pasture. It was a city of refuge, a center of religious and administrative life for the Levites of the tribe of Naphtali.

sens: Fortified city of ancient Israel located at the northwestern border of Judah and the southern border of Benjamin
Place where the Ark of the Covenant was kept for twenty years
H7157.detail:
1. Kirjath-Jearim is an ancient city situated on the borders of two tribal territories: it marks the northwestern limit of Judah and also borders Benjamin to the south. The name means "city of forests," evoking the wooded region where it was located. It is first mentioned in Joshua 9:17 among the Gibeonite cities, and then precisely described in Joshua 18:14 as an important geographical landmark.
2. Kirjath-Jearim became famous as the refuge of the Ark of the Covenant: after the Philistines returned it to Israel, it was deposited there and remained for twenty years (1 Samuel 7:2), before being transferred to Jerusalem by David (2 Chronicles 1:4). It is a place of preservation for what is most sacred, the symbol of God's presence among the people.
H7157.origine: The Hebrew name קִרְיַת יְעָרִים is composed of two words: קִרְיָה (qiryah, "city" or "town") and יַעַר (yaar, "forest"). The second element reflects the geography of the place, covered with dense forests, characteristic of the western Judean highlands. This type of double name, designating a city with its geographical features or history, was common among the ancient Hebrews.
H7157.emploi: Kirjath-Jearim appears nineteen times in the Old Testament, first as a border city in the lists of Joshua (chapters 9, 15, and 18), alongside Gibeon and other Gibeonite cities. It becomes especially important in the account of 1 Samuel, where it serves as the place of custody for the Ark of the Covenant for two decades (1 Samuel 6:21, 7:1-2) — a period of waiting and lamenting before the restoration of worship. It is also mentioned in 1 Chronicles during the transfer of the Ark to Jerusalem. Families from the region are listed in 1 Chronicles 2:53, confirming its administrative significance. It reappears after the exile in Ezra and Nehemiah.
H7157.portee: Kirjath-Jearim reminds us that the presence of God, symbolized by the Ark, could be kept in a humble and distant place from Jerusalem for a long time. Its history illustrates the patience of the people in waiting and shows that God can temporarily dwell far from the central temple. For today's believer, this place evokes that faith perseveres even when worship seems distant or interrupted, and that God prepares restorations.

sens: Fortified city in the territory of Judah, located west of Hebron
Former name of the city of Debir
Place conquered by Caleb and his son-in-law Othniel
H7158.detail:
1. Kirjath-Sépher was a fortified city in the mountainous territory of Judah, located west of Hebron. Its name literally means "city of the book" ("kirjath" = city, "sépher" = book or writing), which may suggest a center of administrative or religious importance. It was inhabited by peoples that the Israelites were to conquer upon entering Canaan (Joshua 15:15).
2. Kirjath-Sépher is simply another name for the city of Debir, as indicated in several passages: "Debir was formerly called Kirjath-Sépher" (Joshua 15:15; Judges 1:11). It is also referred to as Kirjath-Sanna in the list of cities of Judah (Joshua 15:49), a variant of the same name.
3. This city plays a role in the division of territory: Caleb promises his daughter Acsa in marriage to whoever conquers Kirjath-Sépher (Joshua 15:16; Judges 1:12). It is Othniel, Caleb's cousin, who takes up this challenge and thus becomes Caleb's son-in-law, linking this small fortified city to one of the great figures of the time of the Judges.
H7158.origine: The Hebrew name קִרְיַת־סֵפֶר (qiryat sepher) is composed of two words: קִרְיַה (qiryah = "city") and סֵפֶר (sepher = "book" or "writing"). The literal meaning is therefore "city of the book." The origin of the nickname is obscure: perhaps the city housed an important writing or archive center, or the name recalled a forgotten story. What is clear is that this ancient name was replaced by that of Debir, which remains.
H7158.emploi: Kirjath-Sépher appears five times in the Hebrew Bible, always in two parallel passages: Joshua 15:15-16 and Judges 1:11-12, which recount the same conquest and the same challenge from Caleb. It also appears in the list of cities in the territory of Judah (Joshua 15:49), where it is called Kirjath-Sanna. These texts emphasize that it was a fortified city ("will strike," "will take"), a symbol of resistance to the Israelite conquest. The ancient name survives only in these ancient accounts; after the conquest, only the name Debir persists. The episode highlights the strategic importance of the place and its role in the history of Israel's early conquerors.
H7158.portee: Kirjath-Sépher reminds us that the conquest of Canaan was neither instantaneous nor uniform: some cities retained their ancient names for a long time. It also illustrates how God's promises are often fulfilled through the courageous actions of His servants: it is by taking a city that Caleb obtains a son-in-law worthy of his family. This small forgotten city shows us that God accompanies His people in every detail of their journey toward the promised inheritance.

sens: to spread or place something over a surface to cover it
to be covered, to be enveloped by a covering
H7159.detail:
1. The verb expresses the action of putting something over to cover: in Ezekiel 37:6, God says He will cover the resurrected bones with skin, meaning He will spread the skin over them to completely clothe them. It is an act of construction or completion.
2. The passive sense describes the state of being covered: in Ezekiel 37:8, the skin "covered them over," meaning it spread over them and enveloped them. It is the result of the action of covering.
H7159.origine: The verb קָרַם (qaram) comes from a root that originally means "to spread" or "to deploy." The word evokes the concrete image of something that stretches out, unfolds over a surface to completely cover it. It belongs to a semantic field of covering verbs in Hebrew.
H7159.emploi: This verb appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, both in the same passage (Ezekiel 37:6-8), which describes the prophetic resurrection of the dry bones. In the first usage, God speaks to the prophet as the active agent: "I will cover you with skin." In the second, the construction is passive or middle: "the skin covered them over." The context is one of creation or reconstitution of a body, where the verb expresses the step of covering with skin.
H7159.portee: This image of covering with skin conveys God's tenderness in the work of resurrection: He does not merely gather the bones, He carefully clothes them with a living covering. For the believer, this verb reminds us that God restores not only the structures but also the beauty and integrity of the body in the resurrection.

sens: Send out light, shine brightly
Have horns, be equipped with horns
H7160.detail:
1. To shine means to emit light, to radiate. It is the image of an object or a face that shines intensely. Moses comes down from Mount Sinai after encountering God: the skin of his face shines so much that Aaron and the children of Israel are afraid and do not dare to approach him (Exodus 34:29-30). This radiant light is the visible sign of the divine presence that transformed Moses.
2. To have horns or to be equipped with horns: this is the figurative use of the verb applied to animals. A bull with horns is more impressive, more majestic than a defenseless animal (Psalms 69:32). The horns symbolize strength and power.
H7160.origine: The verb קָרַן (qa.ran) comes from a root that evokes the idea of "horn": in Hebrew, the horn of an animal is called קֶרֶן (qe.ren), which comes from the same root. The starting image is that of the horn that points, that shines, that radiates. The verb can therefore mean both "to shine" (like a horn that catches the light) and "to have horns" (literal sense). This dual image shows the deep unity of the word in Hebrew: the horn that radiates.
H7160.emploi: This verb is infrequent in the Bible: only four occurrences. In three of them (Exodus 34:29, 30, 35), it describes the radiance of Moses' face after his encounter with God at Sinai. This is a pivotal moment: the visible transfiguration of Moses shows that divine glory has touched his flesh. One occurrence (Psalms 69:32) uses the verb in the sense of "to have horns" applied to a sacrificial animal. The overall contexts reveal that the verb expresses the manifestation of a power, whether divine (radiance) or natural (animal strength).
H7160.portee: For the believer, the radiance of Moses' face teaches that encountering God visibly transforms the one who has conversed with Him. This glory is not arrogance, but a sign of the work of the Spirit. The veil that Moses must put back on after his encounter (verse 35) emphasizes that the presence of God is both visible and fearsome: it inspires reverent awe. This passage has inspired the theology of the transfiguration of Christ in the Gospels.

sens: Pointed extension on the head of an animal
Container shaped like a horn for holding oil or liquid
Projection in the shape of a horn on the altar of sacrifices
Symbol of strength, power, or victory
Ray or burst of light that radiates
Small height, hill or knoll
H7161A.detail:
1. The horn is the pointed bony protrusion that grows on the heads of certain animals — rams, buffaloes, goats. Abraham sees a ram caught by its horns in a bush (Genesis 22:13), and the psalmist begs God to deliver him from the horns of the buffalo (Psalms 22:22), an image of a threatening and furious beast.
2. A horn also becomes a hollowed or shaped container made from this material: Samuel carries a horn filled with oil to anoint King David (1 Samuel 16:13), a practical and common usage in the ancient Near East.
3. The horns are decorative or sacred projections on the altar: four horns rise at the corners of the altar of burnt offerings and incense (Exodus 27:2; 30:2). The priest puts blood on them for the atonement of sins (Leviticus 4:25), making these horns symbols of purification and grace.
4. The horn represents the strength or power of a person or a nation: "He will exalt the horn of his people" (1 Samuel 2:10) means that God will increase the victory and dominion of His people. Similarly, "your horn will be exalted" (Psalms 89:25) promises the king increased authority.
5. The horn can also evoke a ray of light that bursts forth: Habakkuk speaks of the horns of light, meaning the shining rays in the vision of the Almighty God (Habakkuk 3:4).
6. Rarely, the word designates a small hill or knoll: Isaiah sings "on a fertile knoll" where the vine of his beloved extends (Isaiah 5:1), probably due to its elevated shape resembling a horn.
H7161A.origine: The Hebrew word קֶרֶן (qeren) comes from a root that evokes the pointed and upright shape. The same word exists in Aramaic with the same meaning. In the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint), this word often corresponds to the Greek κέρας (keras), also used in the New Testament to refer to the symbolic horns of the Lamb on the heavenly throne or the power of the Messiah. The horn, throughout the Semitic Near East, naturally embodies the idea of aggressive strength or protection.
H7161A.emploi: The word קֶרֶן appears 68 times in the Old Testament. In the laws of Moses, it primarily refers to the horns of the altar (about thirty occurrences in Exodus and Leviticus): these ritual horns receive the atoning blood and offer refuge to the supplicant who grasps them (1 Kings 1:50; 2:28). In poetry and prophecy, the word shifts to the metaphor of power: the psalms speak of "exalting the horn" of the righteous king (Psalms 89:18, 132:17) or of "breaking the horn" of the wicked (Psalms 75:11). Among the prophets, Ezekiel and Daniel use the horn as a symbol of kingdom or political power (Daniel 8:3-21), announcing future empires. The word is also used plainly for anointing oil (1 Samuel 16:13) and rarely for a topographical relief (Isaiah 5:1).
H7161A.portee: Understanding the horn helps grasp the biblical language of strength and royalty. When the Bible promises to "exalt your horn," it assures visible victory and dominion. Conversely, "breaking the horn of the wicked" signifies their humiliation and downfall. For sacrifices, the horns of the altar remind us that the purifying strength comes from God alone, not from the creature. This rich image remains a language of power and hope in the mouths of the psalmists and prophets.

sens: Region or city of Israel, probably in Bashan
H7161B.detail: Carnain is a place that the people of Israel conquered, likely located in the region of Bashan, east of the Jordan. The name literally means "horns" in Hebrew (in the plural), an image often associated with strength and power in the Bible. This place is mentioned in Amos 6:13, where the prophet reproaches Israel for boasting about small military victories.
H7161B.origine: The Hebrew word קַרְנַיִם (Carnain) comes from the root קֶרֶן (horn), which first designates the pointed appendage of certain animals, then metaphorically strength or power. The name of the place reflects this image: it may be a fortified location or renowned for its power. The same place appears in the compound name "Ashteroth-Carnain" (עַשְׁתְּרֹת קַרְנַיִם), mentioned in Genesis 14:5.
H7161B.emploi: Carnain is attested only once in the provided usages, in Amos 6:13, where the prophet pronounces judgment against Israel in the North. The context shows that Israel boasts of having "taken Carnain by [its] own strength," a victory that the prophet highlights as vanity. The place represents one of the conquests that the northern kingdom was proud of, but which the prophet presents as an illusion of independence from God.
H7161B.portee: Amos rebukes Israel not for winning military victories, but for the pride that arises from them and the forgetting of God behind these successes. This mention invites the reader to examine from what source they believe their successes and strengths come, and not to place their trust in their own exploits rather than in the Lord.

sens: Sharp appendage on the head of an animal
Musical instrument shaped like an animal horn
Symbol of power or strength in prophetic visions
H7162.detail:
1. A horn is the hard, bony growth that certain animals have on their heads, such as bulls or goats. It is a natural part of the animal, often impressive in its shape and hardness.
2. By association with the natural object, trumpets are made by hollowing out an animal horn: it is a musical instrument that produces a loud and deep sound. In Babylon, King Nebuchadnezzar commands the people to fall down at the sound of the horn (trumpet) and other instruments (Daniel 3:5, 3:7).
3. In prophetic visions, particularly those of Daniel, horns become symbols: they represent the power, political strength, or dominion of a kingdom or leader. The terrifying fourth beast has ten horns (Daniel 7:7), and a little horn that comes up among them has eyes and speaks arrogantly (Daniel 7:8), showing that it possesses its own will and power.
H7162.origine: The Hebrew word qeren primarily refers to the horn of an animal, the natural object. The Hebrews observed that this sharp appendage was the visible symbol of the animal's power: the larger the horn, the more impressive and dangerous the animal. They derived a spiritual image from it: the horn represents strength, authority, or dominion. In biblical poetry and prophetic vision, this word becomes a metaphor for political power or the reign of a king.
H7162.emploi: The word horn appears in the Bible mainly in the book of Daniel, where it is used in two ways. First, in the decrees of King Nebuchadnezzar (Daniel 3:5, 3:7, 3:10, 3:15), it refers to the musical instrument that announces the order of worship of the golden statue: the horn (trumpet) is the signal that commands obedience. Second, in the prophetic visions of Daniel (Daniel 7:7, 7:8, 7:11, 7:20, 7:21, 7:24), the horns are symbols of earthly powers or kings: they multiply on a terrible beast (ten horns), and a little horn uproots three others, showing the emergence of a new power that dominates the others. The prophetic context makes the horn the emblem of political strength and dominion.
H7162.portee: For the Christian reader, the horns in Daniel's visions reveal how God sees the powers of this world: they are brute forces, often frightening, but they are also subject to His gaze and control. This image helps the believer understand that earthly kingdoms that seem all-powerful are ultimately just living creatures under God's watch, who can master or destroy them at any moment. It is a comfort for those oppressed by unjust authority.

sens: Daughter of Job, born after his trials
H7163.detail: Keren-Happuch is one of the three daughters that Job had after God restored his life and prosperity (Job 42:14). She is mentioned alongside her sisters Jemima and Keziah, as a sign of the divine blessing granted to Job at the end of his story. Her name means "horn of eye paint" or "horn of antimony," a black powder used for eye makeup — a name evoking beauty and enhancement.
H7163.origine: The name Keren-Happuch is composed of two Hebrew terms: "qéren" means "horn" (by extension, something strong and bright), and "hap-pukh" refers to antimony, a black mineral powder used in ancient times for eye makeup. This name reflects an intention of beauty and radiance, contrasting with Job's previous sufferings and symbolizing renewal and restoration.
H7163.emploi: Keren-Happuch appears only once in the Bible, in Job 42:14. She is cited as the third daughter born to Job after the period of trials and restoration described in the book. Along with her two sisters, she represents the continuation of Job's lineage and testifies to divine generosity: Job receives a new offspring, underscoring the resolution of his story of suffering.
H7163.portee: The name and birth of Keren-Happuch remind the reader that after suffering and trial, God can grant new life, new beauty, and new joy. She embodies the Christian hope in divine restoration and God's kindness towards those who remain faithful to Him despite difficulties.

sens: To bend the knees, to bow down
To bend under a weight, to yield
To fall down, to lose solidity
H7164.detail: 1. The primary meaning is physical: to lean, to lower oneself, to bend the knees — the gesture of one who humbles or bows down. 2. From this comes the idea of bending or yielding under a load: this happens to pack animals when they are overloaded (Isaiah 46:1, where the beasts carry the idols and end up bending under the weight). 3. More broadly, it means to collapse, to lose strength or stability: the Babylonian gods cannot stand, they "collapsed" and fell, powerless before the true power of God (Isaiah 46:2).
H7164.origine: The Hebrew verb קָרַס (qaras) has as its base image the act of bending, lowering oneself, or yielding. It is used only twice in the Bible, which is remarkable: it is precisely to show the impotence of false gods. The root expresses the idea of losing firmness, the ability to stand upright.
H7164.emploi: This verb appears only twice in the entire Hebrew Bible, in verses 1 and 2 of Isaiah 46, in the context of the fall of Babylon. The prophet Isaiah addresses the exiled Judeans: he ridicules the Babylonian gods Bel and Nebo, whose massive idols must be carried on animals. These beasts, overloaded, end up collapsing — and with them, the gods they carry: total impotence. The contrast is striking with the God of Israel, who carries His people (verse 4). The usage is highly symbolic: to collapse is the very image of impotence and falsehood.
H7164.portee: This word teaches us that false gods are merely wood and stone, powerless and destined to collapse, while the one true God carries and supports us. For the believer, it is an assurance: that in which men place their trust, apart from God, will ultimately collapse. Only God is stable and worthy of trust.

sens: Small hook or fastener designed to join two pieces of fabric or material
Connecting element that holds several parts together to form a whole
H7165.detail:
1. A clasp is a small hook, a metal fastener designed to join two pieces of fabric or leather by linking them together. In the construction of the tabernacle, God commands the making of fifty gold clasps to join the fine linen curtains together (Exodus 26:6), thus creating a large continuous surface. It is a concrete and practical object, a simple yet effective fastening mechanism.
2. The clasp serves an assembly function: it transforms several separate elements into a unified whole. Exodus 36:13 recounts how the fifty gold clasps were made and how the curtains were joined together with them, so that the tabernacle formed a complete structure. Without these clasps, the tent would have remained fragmented; with them, it becomes a coherent and stable structure.
H7165.origine: The Hebrew word קֶרֶס (qéres) comes from a root meaning "to attach" or "to fix." It literally designates what hooks and unites. The word only appears in the descriptions of the tabernacle and has no obvious parallel in other Semitic languages: it is a specialized technical term for this liturgical element.
H7165.emploi: The word appears 7 times, all in the book of Exodus, in chapters 26, 35, 36, and 39. It is used solely to describe the clasps of the tabernacle: the gold clasps that join the fine linen curtains of the sanctuary (Exodus 26:6 and 36:13), and the bronze clasps that assemble the goat hair curtains of the roof (Exodus 26:11 and 36:18). The technical term remains stable and precise: it always refers to a metallic object that assembles fabrics or curtains, never in a figurative sense. Even Exodus 26:33, which mentions the veil beneath the clasps, uses them to indicate a spatial reference in the tabernacle.
H7165.portee: The clasp reminds us that the worshiper must enter the tabernacle as a united whole, a gathered people. These small construction details reveal God's thought: nothing is left to chance. The precision and order that prevail in God's house invite the believer to a wholehearted consecration and to understand that the Church is held together by strong bonds established by God Himself.

sens: The joint between the leg and the foot
What allows the foot to move and direct itself
H7166.detail:
1. The ankle is the bony joint that connects the leg to the foot. It is the area where one can feel the prominent bones on each side of the lower leg. In the two passages where this Hebrew word appears (2 Samuel 22:37 and Psalms 18:37), the psalmist says that God enlarges the path under his "steps": it is the ankle that allows the foot to turn and walk confidently on this path.
2. Figuratively, the ankle represents stability and the ability to move forward firmly. When the psalmist asserts that his feet do not slip, he speaks of a moral and spiritual certainty: he can walk straight because God supports him.
H7166.origine: The Hebrew word קַרְסֹל (qarsol) properly designates the ankle joint. The equivalent Greek word is σφυρόν (sphyron), also centered on this fragile yet essential part of the body. The word likely has a root related to the shape of the joint, but its exact etymology remains obscure. It is a specialized term, anatomically precise, rarely used in the Bible.
H7166.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, in two parallel passages: 2 Samuel 22:37 and Psalms 18:37, both composed of a hymn of praise. In both cases, the context speaks of path, walking, and stability: the psalmist thanks God for having made his steps firm. The word thus does not have significant variations in meaning; it remains concrete and anatomical.
H7166.portee: This word reminds us that our ability to advance spiritually rests on solid foundations that only God can establish. The stability of the foot and ankle becomes an image of moral firmness and trust in God: to walk without slipping is to progress in faith without fear.

sens: To rip, shred a fabric, a garment, or a surface
To split, violently open (the sky, mountains)
To remove, snatch away a possession or right from someone
To express mourning or distress by tearing one's clothes
H7167.detail:
1. The primary sense is physical: to rip or shred a fabric, a garment. It is a violent action that destroys the integrity of a cloth. Thus, Saul's mantle is "torn" when Samuel seizes it in passing (1 Samuel 15:27), or the priest's garment must not "be torn" at the neck (Exodus 28:32).
2. By extension, the verb applies to any substance that is violently opened: "to split" the heavens, to make a gaping hole. The prophet pleads: "Oh! that you would tear the heavens and come down" (Isaiah 63:19) — the image is one of dramatic rupture, of a veil being ripped apart.
3. In the language of possession, "to snatch away" means to remove, take from someone what they possess: "It is from your son's hand that I will snatch it away," meaning the kingdom (1 Kings 11:12).
4. Socially and religiously, tearing one's clothes is a gesture of mourning or repentance: Reuben "tears" his clothes upon discovering Joseph's disappearance (Genesis 37:29), and King Josiah "tears" them upon hearing the Lord's words (2 Chronicles 34:27). It is an externalization of pain or remorse.
H7167.origine: The Hebrew verb קָרַע comes from a root that expresses the idea of violent rupture and separation. The word evokes the action of forcing a material to separate into two or to destroy it. It appears in several grammatical forms (such as Niphal "to be torn") that mark the result: a garment that is torn, a fabric that is split. The underlying image is always one of violence that breaks the unity of a thing.
H7167.emploi: The verb "to tear" appears about 60 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the historical books (Samuel, Kings, Chronicles) and in the prophets. Three contexts dominate. First, the physical action: tearing a fabric, a garment, a veil (Exodus 28:32, 1 Kings 11:30). Secondly, the ritual and emotional gesture of mourning: several characters tear their clothes in the face of misfortune or guilt (Genesis 37:29, 2 Samuel 13:19, 2 Chronicles 34:27). Finally, the prophetic image of a cosmic or political rupture: tearing the heavens (Isaiah 63:19), snatching away the kingdom (1 Kings 11:12). The Niphal ("to be torn") describes the resulting state: a fabric that is split, a damaged cloth (Exodus 39:23, Leviticus 13:56).
H7167.portee: This word reminds us that tearing — whether physical or moral — is often a raw expression of human suffering. Tearing one's clothes is to express sorrow when words fail. Conversely, the image of tearing the heavens (Isaiah 63:19) expresses the ardent expectation of a divine intervention that breaks the silence. For the Christian, these passages show how Scripture acknowledges the legitimacy of expressing mourning and contrition, while pointing toward the hope that God Himself can traverse all veils and intervene in history.

sens: Fragment of clothing or fabric that has been torn or ripped
Worn clothing, in tatters, rags
Figuratively: indigence, poverty marked by destitution
H7168.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a fragment of fabric that has been torn or ripped. In the account of Kings, when the prophet Ahijah tears his new cloak into twelve pieces to give ten to Jeroboam, these "pieces" are the parts of the garment he has just lacerated: it is the visible act that accompanies and seals his prophetic word (1 Kings 11:30-31). Similarly, when Elisha takes hold of his clothes and tears them in two after Elijah's ascension, these "pieces" are the parts of his garment that his act of mourning has torn to shreds (2 Kings 2:12).
2. The word can also refer to clothing that is actually worn and torn, rags that cover someone in destitution. This meaning is suggested by the passage in Proverbs: the drunkard and the man who indulges in excess ultimately fall into poverty, and it is "slumbering" — laziness, self-abandonment — that leads him to "wear rags" (Proverbs 23:21). Here, the word does not merely describe an object but the state of one who has fallen into indigence.
3. Figuratively, the word can evoke destruction, destitution, and downfall: one who loses everything possesses only rags.
H7168.origine: The Hebrew word קרע (qéra) comes from a root that means "to tear" or "to lacerate." It is found in the verb "to tear" (קרע, qara), which is very common in the Bible to describe acts of destruction: tearing clothes as a sign of mourning or dismay, tearing a letter, ripping something away. The noun קרע (qéra) is the result of this action — what has been torn, the fragments or rags that result. The basic image is that of rupture, of a violent separation of a fabric.
H7168.emploi: The word appears four times in the Old Testament, always in contexts where it describes either fragments of fabric that have been torn for a significant reason or the state of poverty and destitution. The first three uses concern concrete and symbolic acts: the torn cloak of the prophet Ahijah in two parallel accounts from the First Book of Kings (1 Kings 11:30-31), then the act of mourning by Elisha after Elijah's ascension (2 Kings 2:12). The fourth use, in Proverbs, employs the word more abstractly to evoke the poverty that results from laziness and debauchery. In all cases, the word remains concrete: it always designates torn clothing, either in the literal sense of the fragment or in the sense of the ragged garment that clothes the poor.
H7168.portee: This word reminds the reader that concrete bodily gestures — a torn garment — can carry profound spiritual significance. For Ahijah and Elisha, the fabric that tears expresses a rupture decided by God or a mourning offered before Him. For the poor in rags from Proverbs, the word invites reflection on the link between our choices — laziness, intemperance — and our downfall: one does not wear rags by chance, but as a result of repeated neglect.

sens: Quickly contract the eyes or eyelids
Pinch, squeeze, form by pressing
Make an expressive gesture or revealing mimicry
Insult or show contempt through a look or gesture
H7169.detail:
1. To blink is the action of quickly closing and opening the eyelids — an involuntary or deliberate gesture. In Proverbs 6:13, the dishonest "blinks" to communicate secretly, and in Proverbs 10:10, "he who blinks is a cause of sorrow," showing that this gesture can express malice or duplicity.
2. The verb also means to pinch, squeeze, or form something by pressing. In Job 33:6, Eliphaz says, "I have been shaped like you from clay" — the image is that of clay pinched and pressed to take shape, like a potter shaping his material.
3. More broadly, the word designates any expressive gesture of the body — a blink, a wrinkle, a contraction — that communicates a hidden intention or feeling. In Proverbs 16:30, the one who "bites his lips" and "closes his eyes" combines several gestures to conceal malicious thoughts.
4. Insulting with a look or showing contempt through a mimicry also falls within this scope: in Psalms 35:19, the psalmist asks that "those who hate me without cause do not insult me with their gaze" — that is, do not despise me through their facial expressions and gestures.
H7169.origine: The Hebrew root קָרַץ (qaratz) evokes the idea of pinching, pressing, tightening — as one pinches soft dough to give it shape, or as one quickly closes the eyelids by contracting them. The basic image is that of compression or muscular contraction. The word belongs to a family of bodily expressions: it describes fine and expressive movements of the face or body that betray secret intentions or emotions.
H7169.emploi: The verb appears 5 times in the Hebrew Bible, always in the books of wisdom or poetry (Job, Psalms, Proverbs). Three uses concern blinking: in Proverbs 6:13 and 10:10, it is a sign of cunning and malice; in Psalms 35:19, it is a form of insult. One use (Job 33:6) employs it in the passive to describe the formation of the human body, shaped like clay. A final use (Proverbs 16:30) links it to the gesture of biting one's lips, as an expressive act of a hidden intention. The word thus paints subtle gestures that reveal the heart: in the wicked, they are signals of fraud; in the righteous, they testify to their created nature.
H7169.portee: This word teaches us that small gestures — a blink, a mimic, a look — are never innocent: they express what the heart hides. Proverbs warns us that he who blinks to deceive or insult causes sorrow and walks toward his ruin. Conversely, in Job 33:6, being "formed" from clay reminds us that our bodies, shaped by God, are the place where our souls manifest. Learning to read these gestures — in ourselves and in others — is learning to discern the heart.

sens: Bring an accusation or complaint against someone
Denounce someone to an authority to harm them
Attack someone's reputation with malicious words
H7170.detail:
1. The word primarily means to bring an accusation against someone: it is to come and tell an authority that someone has acted wrongly. In Daniel 3:8, the Chaldeans approach the king to accuse the Jews, that is, to bring a complaint against them.
2. However, it is not a simple objective statement: the word carries the idea of malice. The one who accuses seeks to harm the accused, either through lies or by amplifying the truth. It is a denunciation motivated by hostility or jealousy, as when one "bites" someone with words.
3. The accusation aims to obtain a condemnation from an authority (here the king). It is therefore dangerous and formidable for the one who is the object of it, as it can lead to severe punishment.
H7170.origine: The Hebrew word קְרַץ comes from a root that evokes the idea of biting or tearing with the teeth — hence the image of "attacking" someone. A malicious accusation is like a verbal bite: it wounds, it seeks to devour reputation. This root appears only a few times in the Bible, always to designate this type of hostile and self-interested attack.
H7170.emploi: This word appears twice in the book of Daniel, in chapters 3 and 6, in contexts where jealous enemies denounce God's servants to the king. In Daniel 3:8, the Chaldeans accuse the Jews of having disobeyed the king's decree. In Daniel 6:24, the accusations against Daniel lead to his condemnation to death. In each case, the accusation is presented as unjust or motivated by envy: these are not simple factual reports, but denunciations intended to harm. The term thus always emphasizes the malice of the accuser.
H7170.portee: This word reminds the reader that malice exists — that there are always people ready to accuse others out of jealousy or hatred. It also shows that God's servants can be exposed to unjust accusations (as happens to the Jews and to Daniel). But by placing these accusations in the hands of God, who thwarts or avenges them, the text affirms that the Lord protects His own and that no malicious accusation can triumph against His will.

sens: Stinging insect that torments animals
One who brings ruin and death
H7171.detail: 1. The word primarily refers to an insect or parasite that stings and harasses — a gadfly, a fly that annoys animals. It is an irritating and harmful creature that torments relentlessly. 2. By imagery, it becomes one who brings destruction and death, ravaging like a plague: in Jeremiah 46:20, the king of Babylon invading Egypt is called the "destroyer from the north," like a devastating insect that preys upon its victim.
H7171.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to sting" or "to pinch." Its basic image is that of a stinging or biting insect — a creature that annoys, harms, and torments with its repeated stings. It is the very type of what is bothersome and gradually destructive.
H7171.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 46:20. It refers to King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon invading Egypt as a calamity. There, the image of the gadfly that annoys animals becomes that of the conqueror descending upon a land like a destructive plague, without mercy. It is poetic language: the prophet compares military invasion to the ravages of a fierce parasite.
H7171.portee: This word reminds us that destruction is never chance or accident: it is the consequence of divine judgment. The image of the destroyer from the north also emphasizes that sin and injustice attract judgment like an inevitable plague. For the believer, it is a call to take God's word seriously, for His warnings precede His punishments.

sens: Horizontal surface on which one walks or places objects
Bottom of a place (sea, house)
Lower limit of a space, from bottom to top
H7172.detail:
1. The ground is the horizontal surface, usually of earth, on which one stands. It is the floor or lower level of a building. In Numbers 5:17, the priest takes dust from the ground of the tabernacle to mix it with holy water.
2. By extension, the ground refers to the bottom, the lowest part of any space. In Amos 9:3, the bottom of the sea is called ground: it is the lower limit of the ocean, the deepest place where one cannot go lower.
3. The word also describes a lower limit or boundary in a construction. In 1 Kings 6:30, the "ground of the house" is covered with boards of gold, meaning the interior floor is adorned. In 1 Kings 6:15 and 7:7, the ground is contrasted with the ceiling: it is the starting point from the bottom, from which height is measured to the top of the walls.
H7172.origine: The Hebrew word qarqa' comes from a root that evokes the idea of spreading, flattening. It originally designates what is spread horizontally and on which one can stand. It is a simple and concrete word, deeply rooted in daily life and in the description of buildings.
H7172.emploi: The word appears 6 times in the Hebrew Bible, almost exclusively in descriptive passages of Solomon's temple (1 Kings 6-7) and the tabernacle (Numbers 5). It is used to designate the floor of sacred buildings: in 1 Kings 6:15 and 6:30, the ground of the temple is covered with boards of cedar and then gold; in 1 Kings 6:16, it marks the lower limit of the Most Holy Place. Only once, in Amos 9:3, does it take on a broader meaning and refer to the bottom of the sea, the ultimate point where no creature can escape God. The word remains very concrete and architectural.
H7172.portee: This word reminds us of the material reality of God's dwelling: the tabernacle and the temple are not spiritual abstractions, but tangible buildings, constructed with care and richness. In Amos 9:3, it emphasizes that nowhere on earth or under the earth — from the top of the mountain to the depths of the seas — can one escape divine justice. It is an invitation to take God's presence seriously, both in the sacred and in every corner of creation.

sens: locality on the southern border of Judah
H7173.detail: 1. Karkaa is a locality mentioned only once in the Bible, as a landmark on the southern border of the territory of Judah. It appears in the description of the boundaries of the land assigned to the tribe of Judah after the conquest of Canaan (Joshua 15:3).
H7173.origine: The name Karkaa literally means "ground" or "floor" in Hebrew, derived from the root קרע which evokes what spreads or extends. It is a descriptive geographical name, likely given due to some particularity of the terrain at that location.
H7173.emploi: Karkaa appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 15:3, where it is cited in the enumeration of boundary markers of the territory of Judah. It is situated between several other landmarks — Addar and Hetsron — that mark the southern limit of the tribe towards Egypt. Its exact location is not clearly identified by modern biblical geography, but it represents a strategic point in the southern boundary delineation.

sens: Place located east of the Jordan, in Gilead
H7174.detail: Karkor is a geographical location situated east of the Jordan, in the region of Gilead. It is where the judge Gideon pursued and defeated the Midianite kings Zebah and Zalmunna with the rest of their army (Judges 8:10).
H7174.origine: The name Karkor literally means "foundation" in Hebrew. It likely designates a fortified place or a solid establishment in the desert of the East, from where the leader of the Midianite coalition coordinated his operations.
H7174.emploi: Karkor appears only once in the Bible, in Judges 8:10. It is the site of Gideon's final victory against the Midianites: the judge catches up with the two kings Zebah and Zalmunna who had retreated there with about fifteen thousand warriors, all the survivors of the army that had terrorized Israel. This battle completes Israel's deliverance from the Midianite yoke.

sens: Flat, elongated piece of wood, assembled with others to form a structure
Piece of wood constituting the vertical wall of a construction or furniture
H7175.detail:
1. The word designates a flattened piece of wood, rectangular and elongated, intended to be assembled with others. In the construction of the tabernacle, God commands Moses: "You shall make boards for the tabernacle; they shall be of acacia wood, standing upright" (Exodus 26:15). Each board is a constructive unit, equipped with tenons to fit into frames.
2. By extension, the word designates the vertical elements that form the walls of a structure. The tabernacle has a total of forty-eight: "twenty boards for the second side of the tabernacle, the north side" (Exodus 26:20), assembled by wooden bars that hold them together (Exodus 26:26). Ezekiel also mentions the "boards of cedar" of the ship of Tyre (Ezekiel 27:6).
H7175.origine: The Hebrew word קֶרֶשׁ (qéresh) designates a construction element: a board or a worked piece of wood. Its etymology refers to the idea of squared wood, prepared to be assembled. The word appears mainly in the precise descriptions of the tabernacle and the cultic furniture, where each element has a defined function and measurement.
H7175.emploi: The word appears thirty-four times in the Hebrew Bible, almost exclusively in chapters 26, 36, and 40 of Exodus, which detail the construction of the tabernacle and its dimensions. It is also used in the instructions given to the Levites who were to transport the tabernacle (Numbers 3:36; 4:31). Only one occurrence falls outside this cultic context: the mention of the boards of the ship of Tyre (Ezekiel 27:6). The word is always concrete and technical: it never takes on a figurative meaning in the Bible.
H7175.portee: This word reminds us that God's presence among His people requires precise and meticulous construction. Each board of the tabernacle, assembled with others according to divine orders, illustrates how God desired to be worshiped: not through improvisation, but through obedience to details. For the Christian reader, this evokes divine order and wisdom, and shows that even seemingly ordinary material elements serve God's sacred purpose.

sens: a concentration of houses and inhabitants in one place
an urban and political center, a place of communal life
a human community considered collectively
H7176.detail: 1. The word designates a human settlement, a collection of houses and inhabitants gathered in one place, often organized around a gate (the entrance) and a public square. In Job 29:7, it is at "the gate of the city" that the respected sage stands, a place of meeting and judgment. 2. The city is the center of communal life, with its public places where people gather: the gate, the square, the heights (elevated points of the city). In Proverbs 8:3 and 9:14, wisdom and folly publicly present themselves "at the entrance of the city" and "on the heights of the city" to attract passersby. 3. The city also represents a human community that acts and changes together: it "is exalted by the blessing of the upright" or "is overthrown by the mouth of the wicked" (Proverbs 11:11), showing that the prosperity or downfall of the city depends on the character of its inhabitants.
H7176.origine: The Hebrew word qéret is a feminine noun that designates an urban settlement. It belongs to the fundamental vocabulary of ancient Israel. The context of the provided usages, all drawn from biblical Wisdom (Job and Proverbs), shows that it is a reality very familiar to the Hebrews: a place where one builds, gathers, and lives together.
H7176.emploi: The word qéret appears five times in the provided biblical texts, all in the wisdom books (Job and Proverbs). In Job 29:7, the honored sage sits "at the gate of the city," symbolizing his authority and role as a judge. In Proverbs, the word designates the public place where wisdom and folly present themselves to entice young people (Proverbs 8:3, 9:3, 9:14). Finally, in Proverbs 11:11, the "city" becomes the subject of the verb: it rises or falls according to the morality of its citizens. The usage shows that the word does not simply designate walls and houses, but a living community subject to social and moral dynamics.
H7176.portee: For the believer, this word invites reflection on the link between the moral life of individuals and the prosperity of the community. In Proverbs 11:11, it is clear that the choices of the upright or the wicked affect the common good of the entire city. It is a reminder that our personal righteousness or malice is never without consequence for those around us: we collectively shape the character of our community.

sens: City of the tribe of Zebulun
Possession of the Levites from the family of Merari
H7177.detail: 1. Kartha is a city located in the territory of the tribe of Zebulun, in the Promised Land. It appears in the list of cities allocated to the Levites, those temple servants who did not have a land inheritance like the other tribes (Joshua 21:34). 2. More specifically, Kartha was given to the Levites belonging to the family of Merari, one of the three major branches of the Levitical priesthood. This city and its surroundings constituted their personal possession and allowed them to live off the land while dedicating themselves to the service of God.
H7177.origine: The name "Kartha" comes from the Hebrew קַרְתָּה and simply means "city." It is a generic term that designates an urban settlement. According to tradition, Kartha may also have been known as Kitron, which perhaps suggests a change of name during the ancient history of Israel.
H7177.emploi: Kartha is mentioned only twice in the historical books of the Old Testament: in Joshua 21:34 and in 1 Chronicles 6:77. These two passages are part of the lists of city allocations to the Levites, decided after the conquest of Canaan. Joshua 21 enumerates the cities given to different Levitical families according to their tribe of origin, while 1 Chronicles 6 repeats and completes this information. Kartha is always associated with Jokneam in these enumerations, suggesting geographical proximity.

sens: fortified city in the territory of Naphtali
Levitical city of the Gershonites
H7178.detail: 1. Karthan is a city in the territory of the tribe of Naphtali, in northern Israel. It appears in the land distribution after the conquest, when Joshua allocates several cities with their surroundings for the Levites of the Gershon family to inhabit (Joshua 21:32). 2. As a Levitical city, Karthan was reserved for the priests descended from Gershon, who did not receive their own territory but cities scattered among the other tribes. This organization allowed the Levites to live among the people while remaining separated for the service of the sanctuary.
H7178.origine: The name Karthan literally means "two cities" or "double city," likely evoking its strategic importance or its character as a major urban center. The Bible also refers to it as Kirjathaïm, which also means "double city." It is a site in northern Israel, in the mountainous and fertile region of Naphtali.
H7178.emploi: Karthan appears only once in the Bible: in Joshua 21:32, in the list of Levitical cities. It is cited among the three fortified cities allocated to the Gershonites in the territory of Naphtali, along with Kedesh in Galilee and Hammoth-Dor. This mention is part of the account of the land distribution after the conquest of Canaan, when Moses and Joshua establish the right of habitation for the Levites throughout Israel.

sens: residues of straw left in a field after the harvest
light, dry, and worthless material
anything fragile and ephemeral, destined to be destroyed
H7179.detail: 1. Straw refers to the stalks of grains left in the field after the ears have been cut and removed: this is what the Egyptians forced the Israelites to gather instead of real straw (Exodus 5:12). It is an agricultural residue well known to biblical peoples. 2. By extension, the word describes anything light, fragile, dried, and worthless: a fluttering leaf, a dried blade of straw carried away by the wind (Job 13:25). This is why the image fits things that are contemptible or insignificant. 3. In prophecies, straw becomes the image of destruction and fragility in the face of God's judgment: as a tongue of fire devours the straw (Isaiah 5:24), or as a whirlwind carries it away (Isaiah 40:24), so the wicked are consumed. It is a powerful image of what disappears without resistance.
H7179.origine: The Hebrew word qash comes from the verbal root meaning "to be dry, hard": straw is what remains dry and hard after the harvest. In Hebrew, the same word can also generally refer to straw. The family of this root evokes what is rigid, brittle, hard—qualities of dried straw.
H7179.emploi: The word appears sixteen times in the Hebrew Bible, especially among the prophets and in biblical poetry. It first appears in the story of forced labor in Egypt (Exodus 5:12), where straw replaces the straw provided to the workers. In the poems of Job, it illustrates what is light and weightless (Job 13:25, 41:20). The prophets systematically use it as a figure of judgment: straw burned in fire (Isaiah 5:24, 47:14), carried away by the wind (Isaiah 40:24, 41:2), consumed in the flame (Joel 2:5, Malachi 4:1). It is a consistent comparison that reinforces the contrast between the fragility of man and the power of God.
H7179.portee: This biblical image of straw reminds the reader of human fragility and the futility of resisting God. It teaches that everything that stands against divine justice will be consumed effortlessly, like straw in the fire. For the believer, it is an exhortation not to build one's life on precarious foundations, but on the word of God that endures.

sens: Creeping vegetable plant that produces a long green fruit, eaten as a vegetable
H7180.detail: 1. The cucumber is an elongated green vegetable that the Israelites enjoyed in Egypt: in the desert, they nostalgically remember the cucumbers they freely ate there, alongside melons, onions, and leeks (Numbers 11:5). It was a common and inexpensive food in ancient Egypt, refreshing in a hot climate.
H7180.origine: The Hebrew word קִשֻּׁאָה (qisshual) specifically refers to this vegetable fruit known since antiquity in Egypt and the Middle East. The term appears in lists of provisions and common foods from the ancient world.
H7180.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible. It is found in Numbers 11:5, in the passage where the Israelites, complaining about the monotony of the manna in the desert, regretfully list the varied and appetizing foods they consumed in Egypt. This mention shows that the cucumber was a common and appreciated element of the Egyptian diet.
H7180.portee: This detail reveals how nostalgia for earthly comforts can distract believers from faithfulness to God. The Israelites remember pleasant-tasting foods rather than the miraculous divine intervention that sustains them; the text invites the reader to examine where their desires and regrets lie.

sens: To direct the ear towards someone or something to perceive
To pay attention to a voice, a call, a request
To show attentiveness to advice, a word
To obey by being attentive to what is said
To observe, to pay attention to something
H7181.detail:
1. To listen is primarily to direct one's ear towards a voice or sound. It is to physically or mentally turn to hear: Psalms 10:17 speaks of "bending the ear," a concrete image of this orientation.
2. The word also means "to pay attention," that is, not to let pass what one hears. Jeremiah 8:6 shows the Lord "attentive" to listen to what men do: He does not close His ears; He observes.
3. To listen means "to obey a voice," particularly that of God or an authority. In 1 Samuel 15:22, the "observance" (that is, attentive listening) of God's word is more precious than sacrifices: to truly obey is to have first listened.
4. The word also applies to "taking heed" or "being careful," becoming attentive to a danger or a call. Proverbs 1:24 shows this: when people do not "take heed" to the call of Wisdom, they refuse to take an interest.
5. Sometimes it simply denotes "to observe," to take something into account. Proverbs 29:12 speaks of a king who "pays heed" to lying words: he pays attention, he cares.
H7181.origine: The Hebrew word קָשַׁב comes from a root that evokes the idea of "leaning towards" or "bending to hear." It is a natural image: when one wants to hear someone well, one leans one's ear towards them. The simple form (Qal) carries this sense of orienting oneself to listen. The intensive form (Hiphil) means "to make listen" or "to give attention." This verb is rooted in the physical and immediate experience of hearing.
H7181.emploi: This verb appears 45 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the Psalms, Proverbs, and the prophets. It describes the fundamental attitude that God expects: to listen to His voice. Proverbs uses it to invite receiving teaching: Proverbs 2:2, Proverbs 4:1, 4:20 urge the young man to "listen" to wisdom. The Psalms show that God Himself "listens" to prayers (Psalms 5:3, 86:6, 142:7) and that the believer must "listen" to His words (Psalms 17:1, 61:2). In the prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Zechariah), it is the call to listen to avoid falling into judgment: Jeremiah 6:10 says that the people have no ear to "listen," meaning they do not want to pay attention to the divine warning.
H7181.portee: For the Christian reader, this word speaks to the heart of the relationship with God: to truly listen is more than hearing words; it is to incline in attention and obedience. It is to recognize that God speaks and that my life depends on my receptivity. In 1 Samuel 15:22, this invites not to settle for religious acts but to cultivate a true listening to the Lord. It is also a reminder that God Himself listens to us: our prayers do not fall into a void.

sens: The act of paying attention, concentrating on something
State of listening, vigilance, or watchfulness
Perceptible sign, manifestation that one notices
H7182.detail:
1. Attention is the act of concentrating on something, giving it one's interest. In 1 Kings 18:29, when the prophet Elijah calls on Baal, there is "neither voice, nor answer, nor sign of attention": the deity does not manifest, no one listens or concentrates. It is a total absence of reaction.
2. Attention can also be vigilance or presence of mind. In 2 Kings 4:31, the servant Gehazi places Elisha's staff on the dead child, but "there was neither voice nor sign of attention": no awakening, no lively reaction.
3. It is also a visible sign, a manifestation that can be noticed and observed. In Isaiah 21:7, a watchman "was attentive, very attentive" to the approaching cavalry: she kept her eyes open, she observed with vigilance.
H7182.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to listen" or "to lend an ear." It is related to the physical idea of turning towards something or someone to listen, as one leans the ear to not miss what is said. Attention is therefore primarily a bodily gesture — turning one's attention towards something — that becomes an attitude of the mind.
H7182.emploi: The word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible. In 1 Kings 18:29 and 2 Kings 4:31, it denotes the absence of visible reaction, echo, or sign that someone is listening or acting. It is a non-manifestation, a silence. In Isaiah 21:7, it takes on a positive nuance: the watchman is attentive, showing vigilance and observation. The word thus shows how attention is linked to the presence of a reaction or vigilance: it is to notice, to be there and aware.
H7182.portee: This word reminds us that God notices; He is attentive to our calls and prayers. Conversely, when there is "no sign of attention," it is the absence, the divine silence — as in the case of the false god Baal. For the believer, this invites cultivating one's listening to God, one's spiritual vigilance, knowing that the Lord Himself is attentive to those who cry out to Him.

sens: Who pays attention, who listens with concentration
Who is open and receptive to a request, to a prayer
H7183A.detail:
1. This word describes an ear or a spirit that is fully focused on what is heard — not distracted, not closed, but truly turned towards the one who speaks. Nehemiah asks God: "Let your ear be attentive and your eyes open" (Nehemiah 1:6), as if God's listening could slacken and needed to be invited to turn towards us with all His attention.

2. In a second sense, the word suggests a benevolent disposition, a willingness to take on what is asked of us — not just to hear the words, but to be willing to respond. That is why Nehemiah repeats: "Let your ear be attentive to the prayer of your servant" (Nehemiah 1:11), imploring God not only to listen but to welcome his supplication.
H7183A.origine: This word comes from a Hebrew root (קשב) that originally means "to lean, to incline" — the image of an ear that leans towards the one who speaks, of a spirit that bends to better understand. This root expresses the physical and concrete idea of turning towards someone with intention.
H7183A.emploi: This word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, exclusively in the book of Nehemiah, and always in the mouth of a person addressing God. Nehemiah uses it to implore divine attention: first in Nehemiah 1:6 where he asks God to pay attention to his confessional prayer, then in Nehemiah 1:11 to reiterate his request. The context is that of a pleading prayer where the faithful seeks to ensure that God, in His transcendent majesty, truly listens and intervenes.
H7183A.portee: This word speaks to the heart of the faithful who prays: it reminds us that God is not a distant or distracted listener, but that He can direct His full attention towards us. At the same time, it asks us to believe that our prayer deserves this attention, and it invites us to persevere in supplication, as Nehemiah does.

sens: Who listens attentively, who lends an ear
Who is turned towards someone to hear and understand their request
H7183B.detail:
1. The word describes one who truly listens, who leans in to miss nothing of what is said. It is the attitude of one who concentrates on another's voice. In 2 Chronicles 6:40, King Solomon asks God that His ears be "attentive" to the prayer spoken in the temple: God must truly listen, not just hear in passing.
2. The word also evokes a disposition of the heart: to be attentive is to turn entirely towards someone, to grant them one's full attention. In Psalms 130:2, the psalmist pleads: "Let your ears be attentive to the voice of my supplications!" He asks God not just to listen, but to pay attention, to lean towards him with interest and kindness.
H7183B.origine: The Hebrew root means "to listen" or "to pay attention." The word carries the image of one who inclines his ear, who actively turns towards a voice. It is a call to a lively, conscious, engaged listening — the opposite of distracted listening.
H7183B.emploi: The word appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible, always concerning God. It is used in the solemn prayers of the temple: when Solomon dedicates the temple (2 Chronicles 6:40 and 7:15), he asks God for "attentive" ears to prayer. It is also the language of the psalmist who cries out to God in distress (Psalms 130:2). The word belongs to a high register, that of respectful supplication towards the Lord.
H7183B.portee: This word reminds the reader that God is not an inattentive or indifferent master: He truly listens to those who plead with Him. For the believer in distress, it is a deep comfort to know that God bends His ear towards him. It also invites us to ask ourselves if we listen to God and our brothers with that same benevolent attention.

sens: Vessel or container made of gold intended for libations in the Temple worship
Cup or bowl used to pour ritual liquids on the altar
H7184.detail:
1. In the first two passages (Exodus 25:29 and 37:16), the word refers to a pure gold chalice, one of the sacred utensils that Moses is to make for the Tabernacle. It is a container of a particular shape, set on a base and intended to hold the wine or oil that will be poured as a libation — that is, as a liquid offering poured before God. It is a precious and ritual object, carefully made according to divine instructions.
2. In 1 Chronicles 28:17, David hands over to his son Solomon the plans and models of the gold and silver chalices intended for the new Temple. The word always designates this same type of ritual container, but here it is understood that there are several, used together during the services of the sanctuary.
H7184.origine: The Hebrew word קַשְׂוָה comes from a root that evokes the idea of pressing or emptying. The chalice is literally a container from which the contents are poured — one "presses" it to let the liquid flow. This word belongs to the same family as other terms designating vessels or pouring utensils. In the Greek Old Testament, this word is often rendered by the Greek term for chalice or cup.
H7184.emploi: The word appears four times in the Old Testament, always in connection with the sacred furniture of the Tabernacle and the Temple. It first appears in Exodus 25:29 and 37:16 in the detailed descriptions of the gold utensils that Moses is to have made according to the divine plan. It is also found in Numbers 4:7 in the enumeration of the objects that the Levites are to carry. Finally, 1 Chronicles 28:17 mentions it among the models that David transmits for the construction of Solomon's Temple. In all these contexts, the chalice is treated as an object of great value, made of pure gold or silver, and its use is strictly liturgical: pouring libations before the Lord.
H7184.portee: This chalice of worship reminds the reader that every detail of divine service matters and that God pays careful attention to the beauty and order of His sanctuary. It is an object that consecrates the offering and establishes a visible link between the people and their God. The care taken in its manufacture and transmission, from Moses to David and then to Solomon, illustrates the continuity of reverence for the Lord and the faithful obedience of successive generations.

sens: To be hard, difficult, or burdensome to bear
To become insensitive, impenetrable, or frozen in pride
To harden someone, making them obstinate or rebellious
To show stubborn resistance to the will of God
H7185.detail:
1. This word first depicts concrete hardness: a difficult task that weighs heavily (Deuteronomy 1:17), a hard yoke that crushes (1 Kings 12:4), or the pains of childbirth that stiffen the body (Genesis 35:17).

2. Then it describes the hardening of the heart and soul: to stiffen the neck is to refuse to obey, to block oneself like a statue against God's calls (2 Chronicles 30:8; Nehemiah 9:29).

3. The verb can also mean "to harden": it is the action of someone who voluntarily or involuntarily strengthens another's resistance to grace (Exodus 7:3).

4. Finally, to stiffen the neck is the classic image of spiritual obstinacy, the stubborn refusal to hear, which leads to sudden ruin (Proverbs 29:1).
H7185.origine: The Hebrew verb קָשָׁה (qashah) comes from a root that fundamentally means "to be hard, rigid." The root evokes the hardness of metal or stone, and by extension, the rigidity of the neck and soul. It is related to the adjective קָשֶׁה (qasheh, "hard") and the noun קֹשִׁי (qoshi, "hardness"). The image of the stiffened neck is particularly frequent in the Old Testament to express the stubborn refusal to obey God.
H7185.emploi: This verb appears 28 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the historical and prophetic books. It first denotes material difficulties: hard work, a heavy yoke, the pains of childbirth. But its primary use is spiritual: God hardens Pharaoh's heart to manifest His power (Exodus 7:3), and Israel "stiffens its neck" by rejecting the prophets and the Law (2 Chronicles 36:13; Jeremiah 7:26). The word describes the progressive obstinacy of the people, their growing deafness to calls for repentance. Nehemiah 9:29 shows the escalation: Israel "would stiffen its neck" despite repeated admonitions. Proverbs 29:1 and Psalms 95:8 draw a lesson: he who stiffens his neck will be broken.
H7185.portee: This word reveals the spiritual danger of the progressive hardening of the heart: with each refusal to obey God, one becomes harder, more closed to His voice. It shows that obstinacy is not a mere weakness, but an active revolt against God that leads to ruin. It also invites vigilance: not to stiffen the neck, to remain flexible, docile to God's call, is to place oneself on the path of blessing.

sens: That which resists pressure, modification, which is solid and firm
That which requires much effort, burdensome to endure or accomplish
That which is marked by severity, rigor, or cruelty in behavior or judgment
That which manifests obstinacy, moral rigidity, or rebellion
That which is violent, intense, or brutal in its action or effect
H7186.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of physical solidity: that which does not yield, which is compact and resistant. Joseph speaks "harshly" to his brothers (Genesis 42:7), meaning with a firm voice and a cold attitude that will not bend.
2. The word then describes what is difficult, painful to endure: slavery in Egypt was "hard" (Exodus 1:14), meaning oppressive and merciless for those who endured it.
3. It characterizes a severe and uncompassionate attitude or judgment: when a king responds "harshly" to his people (2 Chronicles 10:13), he refuses to listen to them and imposes his will rigidly.
4. In the prophetic words of Moses, it describes the spiritual obstinacy of the people: "the stiff neck" (Exodus 33:3) symbolizes the refusal to submit to God, a moral rigidity that resists all correction.
5. Finally, it expresses violence and intensity: a "very fierce" battle (2 Samuel 2:17) is a fierce fight, where the blows are violent and merciless.
H7186.origine: The Hebrew word קָשֶׁה (qasheh) comes from a root denoting hardness and resistance. It evokes the image of that which does not yield, which refuses to bend. In the Hebrew Bible, it applies both to material (that which is hard to the touch) and to will (that which refuses to bend), as well as to the heart (that which refuses to obey or to show compassion). It is a very concrete word, rooted in the sensory experience of the hard and the solid.
H7186.emploi: This word appears 36 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the historical books and the prophets. It first describes material or physical realities: a fierce battle, a harsh voice. But very often, it characterizes the people of Israel in relation to God, particularly their obstinacy in not listening to the voice of the Lord: the people with the "stiff neck," rebellious and unyielding (Exodus 33:3; Deuteronomy 9:6, 9:13; Ezekiel 2:4, 3:7). The prophets also use it to describe terrible punishments: kingdoms that oppress with harshness (Isaiah 19:4), judgments without mercy. Its meaning varies little, but the context shifts from the concrete (a material, a battle) to the figurative (the heart, the will).
H7186.portee: This word reminds the reader that the hardness of heart is the great obstacle to a relationship with God. When Israel shows itself to be "stiff-necked," it is their refusal to obey that displeases the Lord, not merely their weakness. For the believer, it is an invitation to examine one's own heart: have I become "hard" in response to God's voice? Hardness can also refer to the sufferings and oppressions of the world, reminding us that the Lord alone can free us from the hard yoke.

sens: That which is in accordance with reality, without lie or deception
That which is authentic, trustworthy
That which is just and right in actions and ways
H7187.detail:
1. Truth is what corresponds to real facts, what does not deceive. When King Nebuchadnezzar says to Daniel, "truly, your God is the God of gods," he acknowledges that this statement corresponds to reality: Daniel's God is truly powerful and really reveals secrets (Daniel 2:47).
2. This word also denotes the character of what is authentic and worthy of trust. All of God's works are "true," meaning trustworthy, conforming to what they promise (Daniel 4:37).
3. Truth is expressed in the justice and righteousness of ways: the king recognizes that God's ways are "true," just and right, without deviation or injustice.
H7187.origine: This Aramaic word is very close to the Hebrew qoshet (קֹשְׁטְ), which also means "truth." Both forms trace back to a root that evokes the notion of that which is solid, established, durable — the image of something that "stands firm" and does not collapse. Truth is that which withstands the test, that which remains reliable.
H7187.emploi: This Aramaic word appears twice in the book of Daniel, in chapters 2 and 4, in contexts of recognition of God's power and reliability. King Nebuchadnezzar uses it to express the certainty that Daniel's God is real and truly acts. The word marks a solemn confession: it is the recognized and proclaimed truth, not a mere opinion. Daniel, a prophet in a foreign land, receives this confession from the mouth of the pagan king himself, which shows that God's truth imposes itself on all, even the powerful of the world.
H7187.portee: This word from the king reminds us that God's truth is not a matter of opinion or personal belief, but a reality that even adversaries must recognize. God's ways are just and trustworthy: one can rely on them. When we go through trials or doubts, this established truth offers us a solid foundation.

sens: Make hard, insensitive, resistant
Treat with harshness, without mercy
Make the heart impervious to the fear or obedience of God
H7188.detail:
1. The word primarily evokes physical hardness: to make something hard, solid, or resistant. One can also speak of a hard behavior, lacking sensitivity. In Job 39:19, the ostrich is described as "hard" towards its young, indifferent to their fate: this is a hardness of heart, an absence of pity.
2. By extension, to treat someone harshly, roughly, without consideration. It is to inflict a difficult trial, a severe treatment.
3. In a spiritual sense, to harden the heart means to make it impervious to God, closed to His fear, His love, His call. In Isaiah 63:17, the prophet reproaches the Lord for having "hardened" the heart of the people against His fear: the people become incapable of returning to God, frozen in rebellion.
H7188.origine: The Hebrew verb קָשַׁח comes from a root that expresses the idea of hardening, making rigid or insensitive. It belongs to the same family as other Hebrew words describing hardness or severity. The basic image is that of a material hardening, losing its flexibility and responsiveness — an image that the Bible transposes to the human heart to describe its refusal to obey or repent.
H7188.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Job 39:19, it characterizes the attitude of the ostrich towards its young: it treats them harshly, with cruel indifference. In Isaiah 63:17, it is the key verb in a prayer where the prophet asks God why He has hardened the heart of His people against Him. In this context, hardening the heart is the mysterious action by which God makes a people impervious to His voice, incapable of turning to Him. It is an image of judgment: God abandons the people to their own hardness.
H7188.portee: This word reveals a formidable truth: the human heart can become a heart of stone, closed to God, insensitive to His call. For the Christian, it serves as a reminder of the danger of progressively hardening oneself through disobedience, doubt, or contempt. The Bible warns that persisting on this path leads to a judgment where God "will deliver" the rebellious heart to its own hardness. The call is to embrace grace before the heart becomes irreparably closed.
